items.title: Semgrep benchmarks show GLM 5.2 outperforms Claude Code in IDOR vulnerability detection with 39% F1 score versus 32%, using open-weight model from Zhipu AI [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GLM 5.2 beats Claude in our benchmarks
items.summary:
Semgrep's recent benchmarks reveal that GLM 5.2, an open-weight model from Zhipu AI, outperforms Claude Code in detecting Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) vulnerabilities, achieving a 39% F1 score compared to Claude Code's 32%. This evaluation used the same dataset and prompt across models, highlighting GLM 5.2's competitive edge despite lacking the specialized harness that boosts Semgrep's own multimodal pipeline to 53–61% F1.

GLM 5.2 stands out due to its open-weight availability under an MIT license, allowing security teams to run and fine-tune it internally. It features a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 750 billion parameters and supports extended context lengths up to one million tokens, which is beneficial for complex security tasks. Additionally, its cost efficiency is notable, operating at roughly one-sixth the price of comparable frontier models. These factors make GLM 5.2 a promising option for AI-driven vulnerability detection in security workflows.

items.title: Brown University professor reports mass AI cheating by at least 50 students on March midterm exam in advanced economics course [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Professor denounces mass AI fraud on an exam at Brown
items.summary:
Professor Roberto Serrano of Brown University has uncovered widespread cheating involving artificial intelligence by at least 50 students during the March midterm exam in his advanced economics course. This incident represents the largest known academic integrity breach at Brown and across the Ivy League. Despite presenting conclusive evidence, Serrano reported receiving minimal response from university leadership, prompting calls for a more serious and transparent approach to addressing AI-related cheating.

The course, which traditionally enrolls fewer students, saw an unusual increase to 86 participants this semester, likely due to a new take-home exam format. The midterm results were unusually high, with many answers matching AI-generated content. In response, the final exam was held in person, resulting in significantly lower scores and attendance. Serrano emphasizes the need for open discussion and stronger measures to uphold academic standards in the face of evolving AI challenges.

items.title: User employs Claude Code with Opus 4.8 to analyze MRI results, finds AI diagnosis contradicts human report on shoulder tendon tear [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I used Claude Code to get a second opinion on my MRI
items.summary:
A user with shoulder pain used Opus 4.8 within Claude Code to analyze their MRI results and obtain a second opinion on a diagnosis of a partial-thickness tear in the subscapularis tendon. The AI analysis contradicted the human medical report by finding the tendon intact, prompting further comparison between the two assessments. The AI arbiter favored the AI reader's conclusion, identifying mild tendinosis but no tear, raising questions about the initial diagnosis and treatment plan.

The user detailed their experience setting up the AI analysis, including providing limited clinical context and allowing the AI to install necessary packages for MRI data processing. They also noted concerns about the original treatment, such as the use of shockwave therapy and homeopathic injections, which were flagged by another AI model. Despite the AI's decisive verdict, the user remains uncertain about fully trusting AI over human experts and is considering further medical consultation or continued rehabilitation.

This case highlights the potential and current limitations of AI in medical diagnostics, illustrating how AI can challenge traditional diagnoses but also create uncertainty for patients. It underscores the need for cautious integration of AI tools in healthcare and the importance of expert oversight in interpreting AI-generated findings.

items.title: Researchers introduce Proxy-KD method to improve knowledge distillation from black-box large language models, outperforming traditional white-box techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge Distillation of Black-Box Large Language Models (2024)
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Proxy-KD, a new method to improve knowledge distillation from black-box large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4. This approach uses a proxy model to facilitate effective knowledge transfer to smaller models, overcoming the challenge of inaccessible internal states in proprietary LLMs. Experiments demonstrate that Proxy-KD not only enhances distillation from black-box teachers but also outperforms traditional white-box techniques.

The Proxy-KD method offers a promising solution for leveraging the capabilities of advanced LLMs without requiring access to their internal mechanisms. This advancement could accelerate the development of smaller, more efficient models that retain high performance by learning from powerful but opaque teacher models.

items.title: OpenAI Codex issue to add file exclusion mechanism for sensitive data remains open as of June 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A way to exclude sensitive files issue still open for OpenAI Codex
items.summary:
An open issue on OpenAI Codex's GitHub repository highlights the need for a feature that allows users to exclude sensitive files from being read or sent to the model. This mechanism would enable explicit marking of files or paths to be ignored at both repository and global levels, such as .env or .ssh directories, to protect sensitive data and improve security.

The proposal suggests a deterministic and shareable configuration system, like a .codexignore file, that can be used across teams and projects. Although a related issue was previously closed in favor of a Rust implementation, as of mid-2026, no equivalent feature exists, prompting renewed discussion and interest in developing this functionality.

items.title: Researchers propose DysLexLens, a low-resource LLM framework analyzing dyslexic learners' AI tool experiences via Reddit forums with dictionary filtering and knowledge-graph reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners Insights from Online Forums
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DysLexLens, a low-resource large language model (LLM) framework designed to analyze the experiences of dyslexic learners using AI tools by examining discussions on Reddit forums. The framework transforms noisy social media posts into a focused corpus using dictionary-driven filtering, applies knowledge-graph-based reasoning for semantic analysis, and generates verifiable responses that are evaluated through both quantitative metrics and human assessment.

DysLexLens features four main components: a filtering method to improve data relevance, integration of LLM-assisted semantic analysis with knowledge-graph query reasoning, quantitative evaluation metrics to assess response quality, and structured guidelines for qualitative validation focusing on hallucination and evidence alignment. The framework was tested on dyslexia-related Reddit data with 30 questions, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential applicability to other low-resource online forum contexts. The researchers have made DysLexLens, along with sample data and evaluation results, publicly available on GitHub to support reproducibility.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dyslexic learners increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support reading, writing, organisation, and study-related tasks. However, their lived experiences with these tools remain largely underexamined. This paper proposes DysLexLens, a low-resource LLM framework, designed to analyse dyslexic learners experience with AI through online forum discussions. DysLexLens is designed as an end-to-end, evidence-traceable architecture which transforms noisy social media posts into a dictionary-driven corpora, provides knowledge-graph (KG)-based question reasoning, generates verifiable query responses, and enables response evaluation through quantitative and human-grounded assessment. DysLexLens has four key features. First, it employs a dictionary-driven filtering method to construct a more focused Reddit corpus on dyslexia and AI, filtering out noisy and weakly related posts to improve the relevance of data collected from low-resource forum contexts. Second, it integrates LLM-assisted semantic analysis with KG-based query reasoning to uncover meaningful patterns. Third, it has quantitative evaluation metrics (RAGAS and Query Robustness) to measure LLM-generated response performance. Fourth, it provides structured qualitative validation guidelines for assessing response quality, with a specific focus on hallucination and evidence alignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DysLexLens using dyslexia-related Reddit forum data and 30 questions. The results show its potential generalisability to other low-resource forum data contexts. DysLexLens, sample data, questions and evaluation results are available at Github to support reproducibility.

items.title: Researchers argue that the term machine unlearning is overused in large language model research and should be reserved for dataset-defined deletion with retraining equivalence guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Position: The Term "Machine Unlearning" Is Overused in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers argue that the term "machine unlearning" is often misapplied in large language model (LLM) research and should be specifically reserved for the process of dataset-defined deletion. This involves removing the influence of a precisely specified subset of training data so that the resulting model closely resembles one retrained without that data. They highlight that many current uses of "unlearning"—such as refusal of harmful requests or targeted knowledge suppression—serve different, policy-driven goals and thus require distinct terminology and evaluation methods.

The paper emphasizes that conflating these different objectives under the same label leads to confusion and misuse of metrics and benchmarks, which may reward superficial indicators rather than true retraining equivalence. The authors call for clearer terminology tied to explicit guarantees and reference models, along with evaluations that align with the specific objectives claimed by each approach.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly face demands to "forget" training data, knowledge, or behaviors due to regulatory deletion obligations, copyright/licensing disputes, and safety or product-policy requirements. This position paper argues that machine unlearning is overused as a term in LLM research and should be reserved for dataset-defined deletion: removing the training influence of a precisely specified forget set such that the resulting model is approximately indistinguishable from retraining without that data. We contend that many tasks currently labeled "unlearning" (e.g., refusal for harmful requests, entity/knowledge removal, or targeted suppression) pursue different, often policy-dependent objectives and therefore require different terminology and baselines (e.g., alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation). We further argue that this confusion is not cosmetic: because papers make different implicit guarantees under the same label, metrics and benchmarks are frequently reused outside their intended scope, rewarding surface-level non-disclosure (e.g., low ROUGE/forget accuracy) even when retraining-equivalence is not tested and derived capabilities remain. We conclude by calling for stricter terminology tied to explicit guarantees and reference models, and for evaluations that match the claimed objective.

items.title: Researchers release Supersede, a reinforcement-learning environment to diagnose and train memory-update gaps in LLM agents, improving fact currency accuracy from 9.0% to 16.7% on real conversations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Supersede: Diagnosing and Training the Memory-Update Gap in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Supersede, a reinforcement-learning environment designed to address the challenge of memory-update gaps in large language model (LLM) agents during long, multi-session interactions where facts change over time. Their study reveals that even advanced models like GPT-5.4 experience significant accuracy drops when relying on bounded, self-maintained memory instead of full context, highlighting a persistent issue in memory maintenance rather than comprehension. Supersede rewards agents for using current facts and penalizes outdated information, providing a novel training signal to improve temporal fact accuracy.

Testing Supersede with a smaller open model, Qwen2.5-3B, demonstrated that fine-tuning nearly doubled the model's accuracy in handling updated facts during real conversations, increasing from 9.0% to 16.7%. This marks the first evidence that the supersession gap—difficulty in updating and maintaining current facts—can be effectively trained down rather than merely measured. The environment and findings offer a new approach to enhancing LLM agents' ability to manage evolving information in dynamic conversational settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents operate over long, multi-session interactions in which facts change: a user moves, a price updates, a plan is revised. Acting correctly requires using the current value of a fact and discarding values that have been superseded. We isolate this ability on real conversational data and show that it is a distinct, unsolved failure. On the knowledge-update subset of LongMemEval, replacing an agent's full context with a bounded, self-maintained memory drops accuracy from 92% to 77% even on a frontier model (gpt-5.4), a gap that is statistically significant (paired McNemar p<0.005) and persists across model scale while full-context accuracy saturates near 92%. The bottleneck is therefore memory maintenance, not comprehension, and is not closed by a stronger model. We then ask whether this is merely an undersized memory, and find it is not: as the conversation grows 24x, accuracy falls further (from 68% to 28%), and granting the agent proportionally more memory yields no detectable recovery (28% to 28%, n=25). The failure scales with the length of the conversation, not the compression ratio. We release Supersede, an open reinforcement-learning environment (on the verifiers / prime-rl stack) that turns this measurement into a training signal: agents are rewarded for answering from the current value and penalized for stale ones. Finally, we close the loop and show the gap is trainable: GRPO fine-tuning a small open model (Qwen2.5-3B) on this environment nearly doubles its held-out supersession accuracy on real, unseen conversations (9.0% to 16.7%, a single run), along a monotonic checkpoint curve indicating the learned policy, not the harness, carries the gain. To our knowledge this is the first trainable environment whose reward targets temporal fact-currency, and the first evidence the supersession gap can be trained down, not only measured.

items.title: Researchers introduce MMEE corpus and benchmark speech emphasis models across 7 languages and 34 emotions, finding multilingual training improves robustness and cross-emotion transfer is strong [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Speech Emphasis Models Generalize across Languages and Emotions?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis) corpus, comprising 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances across seven languages and 34 emotion or style categories, to study prosodic emphasis in speech. They evaluated two advanced speech emphasis detection models under various conditions, including monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, and cross-emotion settings, revealing that multilingual training enhances model robustness compared to monolingual approaches, which struggle with zero-shot transfer especially across typologically distant languages.

The study found that models transfer effectively between high- and low-arousal emotions and that there is a shared prosodic structure between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks, as indicated by bidirectional transfer. Additionally, the models maintained strong performance even with smaller training datasets, suggesting potential for efficient training across diverse linguistic and emotional contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prosodic emphasis varies across languages, emotions, and speaking styles, yet existing emphasis detection models are largely trained and evaluated on monolingual neutral read speech. We introduce MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis), a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances (14.13 hours) across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual labels (10 annotations per sample). We benchmark two state-of-the-art architectures under monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and data-scale settings. Monolingual models show limited zero-shot transfer, degrading across typologically distant languages, while multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions; bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks suggests shared prosodic structure; and performance stays robust even at smaller training scales.

items.title: Researchers propose Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD) to improve numerical prediction accuracy in large language models across mathematical and visual tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Numerical Prediction in LLMs via Smooth MMD Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD), a novel training objective designed to enhance the numerical precision of large language models (LLMs). Unlike standard cross-entropy loss, which treats numeric tokens as unrelated categories, SMMD incorporates value-distance kernels and graph-based smoothness to better align predicted numeric distributions with target values. This approach addresses the challenge of LLMs producing unreliable outputs when exact numerical accuracy is required.

The team evaluated SMMD across four tasks involving numeric targets—mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, and chart question answering—using various open-weight LLM and vision-language model backbones. Results showed consistent improvements in accuracy over traditional cross-entropy and recent numeric-target loss functions. Analyses highlighted the complementary benefits of combining maximum mean discrepancy with smoothness and emphasized the importance of designing distance-based kernels. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite their strong general capabilities, large language models (LLMs) often remain unreliable when outputs must be numerically precise. A key reason is the training objective: standard cross-entropy treats numeric tokens as unstructured categories and ignores the metric structure of their values. We address this mismatch with Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD), which builds on the classic MMD by incorporating value-distance kernels over numeric tokens and graph-based smoothness. With this kernel defined over a numeric sub-vocabulary, SMMD aligns the predicted numeric distribution to the target via kernel matching and smooths the prediction-target residual over the induced kernel graph to encourage local consistency. We evaluate SMMD on four numeric-target tasks: mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, and chart question answering, across multiple open-weight LLM and VLM backbones. SMMD consistently improves accuracy over both cross-entropy and recent numeric-target losses; analyses show complementary effects between MMD and smoothness and underscore the importance of distance-based kernel design. Code is available at https://github.com/Zuozhuo/smmd-loss.

items.title: Researchers introduce VASAE, a vocabulary-aligned sparse autoencoder that assigns intrinsic token names to Transformer features without reducing reconstruction quality, aligning about 90% of features in GPT-2-small layers 0-10 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VASAE: Naming SAE Dictionary Directions with Vocabulary-Aligned Anchoring
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Vocabulary-Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (VASAE), a method that trains sparse autoencoder features to align directly with a Transformer's token vocabulary by assigning each feature an intrinsic token name based on the nearest token embedding. VASAE maintains reconstruction quality comparable to standard sparse autoencoders while producing dictionaries with vocabulary-aligned features, achieving about 90% alignment in GPT-2-small layers 0 to 10 and strong alignment in shallow and middle layers of Llama-3.1-8B.

The study shows that after adjusting for sentence-level mean sparse codes, many intrinsic token names correspond closely to nearby input tokens, suggesting that vocabulary-aligned anchoring effectively connects learned features to token identities during training. This approach complements traditional post hoc interpretations of learned dictionaries and enhances understanding of Transformer residual stream decompositions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide useful decompositions of Transformer residual streams, but their learned features are usually named post hoc rather than directly connected to the Transformer's token vocabulary. We introduce Vocabulary-Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (VASAE), a method that trains SAE features under vocabulary-aligned anchoring and assigns each feature an intrinsic token name: the token string whose embedding is nearest to that feature. Without reducing reconstruction quality compared with a standard SAE, VASAE produces dictionaries with vocabulary-aligned features. Using a 0.8 cutoff on the nearest-token alignment score, dictionaries trained on GPT-2-small post-residual streams align about 90% of features in layers 0--10. In Llama-3.1-8B, representative shallow and middle-layer dictionaries contain strongly aligned features, including 92.8% in the shallow layer, while the representative final-layer dictionary shows limited alignment. After subtracting the sentence-level mean sparse code, case studies show that many remaining intrinsic token names are relevant to nearby input tokens. These results suggest that vocabulary-aligned anchoring can connect learned features to intrinsic token names during training, complementing post hoc interpretation of learned dictionaries.

items.title: Researchers propose MultiHashFormer, a hash-based generative language model framework enabling autoregression with constant parameter footprint, outperforming standard Transformers at 100M to 3B scales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MultiHashFormer: Hash-based Generative Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MultiHashFormer, a novel hash-based generative language model framework that enables autoregressive processing with a constant parameter footprint. Unlike traditional language models that use large embedding matrices scaling with vocabulary size, MultiHashFormer represents each token as a unique hash signature composed of multiple discrete hash IDs. This approach allows the model to compress token representations efficiently and generate the next token's hash signature, which is then decoded back to text.

The team evaluated MultiHashFormer at parameter scales of 100 million, 1 billion, and 3 billion, finding that it consistently outperforms standard Transformer language models across various benchmarks. Additionally, the model supports multilingual vocabulary expansion without increasing its parameter footprint or requiring modifications, highlighting its scalability and efficiency for diverse language tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models (LMs) represent tokens using embedding matrices that scale linearly with the vocabulary size. To constrain the parameter footprint, prior work proposes hashing many tokens into a single vector within encoder-only models. While this offers parameter efficiency, many-to-one collisions prevent its use in causal LMs. In this paper, we propose MultiHashFormer, a new framework that allows hash-based autoregression. Each token is represented as a unique hash signature, a short sequence of discrete hash IDs, generated by multiple independent hash functions. A Hash Encoder compresses this signature into a single latent vector for processing by a Transformer decoder. Then, a Hash Decoder generates the hash signature of the next token, which is then mapped back to text. We evaluate our approach at the 100M, 1B and 3B parameter scales, demonstrating that MultiHashFormer consistently outperforms standard Transformer LMs across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that our model handles multilingual vocabulary expansion with a constant parameter footprint without any modifications.

items.title: arXiv:2606.28127 argues large language models are a special case of world models with a continuous spectrum from token prediction to latent-space architectures, examining data and architecture challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Tokens to States: LLMs as a Special Case of World Models and the Continuous Path Beyond
items.summary:
The paper on arXiv titled "From Tokens to States: LLMs as a Special Case of World Models and the Continuous Path Beyond" challenges the common view that large language models (LLMs) and world models are fundamentally different. It argues that LLMs are a specific, limited form of world models where the state space consists of token sequences and actions involve appending tokens. The authors propose a continuous spectrum of models bridging token prediction and latent-space architectures, with intermediate approaches like multi-token and future-summary prediction already explored in current research.

The paper also discusses two key challenges in advancing beyond traditional LLMs: the availability of large-scale self-supervised data versus the need for instrumented, action-labeled environments, and whether transformer architectures can generalize to continuous-state prediction or if new model primitives are necessary. These issues highlight open research questions about data sources and architectural design in the pursuit of more general intelligence models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The AI community has framed the relationship between large language models (LLMs) and world models as a dichotomy: LLMs predict tokens; world models simulate reality. Yann LeCun argues in 2022 that reaching general intelligence requires abandoning autoregressive token prediction in favour of latent-space architectures. This framing is unnecessarily binary. Two claims will be defended. First, LLMs are a degenerate special case of world models: the state space is the set of all token sequences, the only action is appending one token, and world models are therefore a strict generalisation of LLMs, not a replacement. Second, there is a natural continuous spectrum from NTP to JEPA, with multi-token prediction, future-summary prediction, and next-latent prediction as intermediate stations already populated by current research. Moving along this spectrum relaxes the LLM constraints one by one. It also progressively surrenders the two practical advantages that make LLMs trainable at scale: internet-scale self-supervised data, and a transformer architecture co-designed for discrete token prediction. Both are examined as open research questions: the data question (the cliff from self-supervised text to instrumented action-labelled environments) and the architecture question (whether the transformer generalises to continuous-state prediction, or whether a new primitive is needed).

items.title: Researchers introduce Epi2Diff framework using LLM reasoning traces to predict human item difficulty with interpretable cognitive episodes, outperforming baselines on four datasets including SAT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Epi2Diff, a novel framework that uses reasoning traces from large language models (LLMs) to predict human item difficulty in educational assessments. By converting LLM reasoning into cognitively meaningful episodes, Epi2Diff models difficulty based on problem-solving effort and state transitions, offering an interpretable approach beyond traditional text-based methods. The framework outperforms existing baselines across four datasets, including SAT benchmarks, demonstrating an 8.1% average relative improvement over supervised LLM fine-tuning.

Epi2Diff groups segments of reasoning traces into functional problem-solving states, capturing dynamics such as reasoning scale and effort allocation. Experiments reveal that more difficult items trigger more complex and iterative cognitive episodes rather than simply longer responses. This approach provides a scalable and interpretable process representation for understanding item difficulty, potentially enhancing fairness and effectiveness in educational measurement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting human item difficulty is central to educational assessment, where reliable estimates support fairness and effective test construction. Existing methods often depend on costly human calibration or item-level textual representations, providing limited evidence about the cognitive processes that make items difficult. We argue that difficulty should be viewed not only as a property of item text, but also as an observable consequence of the problem-solving burden an item induces. Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) offer scalable process evidence through reasoning traces, but such evidence must be structured to support interpretable modeling. To this end, we introduce Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty), a framework that maps LRM reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences. These episodes group trace segments into functional problem-solving states, enabling difficulty to be modeled through reasoning scale, effort allocation, and state transitions. Epi2Diff extracts compact episode-dynamic features and combines them with semantic item representations for human difficulty prediction. Experiments on four real-world human difficulty datasets show that Epi2Diff consistently outperforms strong baselines, including fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, Epi2Diff achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning baselines. Further analyses show that harder items induce more effortful, iterative, and implementation-centered episode dynamics, rather than merely longer responses. These results demonstrate that cognitive episodes in LRM reasoning traces provide a predictive and interpretable process representation for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement with reasoning models.

items.title: Google introduces Paper Assistant Tool to automate scientific peer review, improving error detection by 34% and piloting at STOC and ICML conferences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool
items.summary:
Google has developed the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), an AI-powered system designed to automate and enhance the scientific peer review process. PAT analyzes full scientific manuscripts to evaluate theoretical results, validate experiments, suggest improvements, and detect potential errors, achieving a 34% improvement in identifying mathematical errors compared to previous methods. The tool has been piloted at major computer science conferences, including STOC and ICML, where it has successfully identified critical issues and helped improve research papers before submission.

By integrating PAT into the review workflow, Google aims to address the growing challenge of scaling traditional peer review to keep pace with the rapid increase in AI-assisted scientific research. The tool reduces the cognitive load on human reviewers while maintaining their oversight, potentially accelerating the verification and publication of scientific findings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving a revolution in scientific discovery, accelerating everything from hypothesis generation to mathematical theorem proving. However, this rapid acceleration is creating a systemic challenge: traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the influx of AI-assisted science. Ultimately, to resolve this tension, we must also deploy AI to accelerate the verification and review process itself. To frame the discussion around this transition, we propose a taxonomy consisting of four progressive levels of AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation, and discuss various trade-offs involved with each. As a step toward this future, we introduce the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), an agentic AI framework built for deep scientific review and verification. PAT ingests full scientific manuscripts and produces a comprehensive evaluation, checking theoretical results, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, and identifying potential flaws. By utilizing inference scaling techniques, PAT is able to identify deeper issues than a single model call alone, achieving a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical errors in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments of PAT as a pre-submission tool for authors at two major Computer Science conferences -- STOC and ICML -- demonstrate its ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements to research papers. By catching errors early, PAT eases the cognitive burden placed on referees, while preserving their control over the outcomes of the review process.

items.title: Researchers introduce LiveClawBench, a benchmark with 134 executable cases across 10 domains to evaluate LLM agents on complex, real-world assistant tasks with stateful execution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LiveClawBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Complex, Real-World Assistant Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LiveClawBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents on complex, real-world assistant tasks that require stateful execution. The benchmark addresses the challenge of fidelity in evaluation by combining a Triple-Axis Complexity Framework for task difficulty with reproducible full-stack mock applications that maintain execution semantics. LiveClawBench includes 134 executable cases across 10 domains and 22 mocked services, enabling controlled and extensible assessment of realistic agent behaviors.

LiveClawBench overcomes limitations of existing benchmarks, which often simplify task distributions or environments, by preserving real-world complexities such as cross-service dependencies, contaminated state, implicit intent, and runtime changes. The benchmark resources, including the benchmark itself, a leaderboard, and task trajectories, have been made publicly available to support further research and development in LLM-based personal assistants.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.13072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: OpenClaw-style personal assistants extend LLM agents from isolated tool use to open-ended, stateful, and personalized software environments. Evaluating these assistants is fundamentally a fidelity problem: benchmarks must be faithful both to the distribution of real assistant tasks and to the execution semantics of the environments in which those tasks unfold. Existing benchmarks often lose fidelity in one dimension or the other. Their task distributions are shaped by what is easy to isolate, mock, and verify, underrepresenting real-world difficulties such as cross-service dependency, contaminated state, implicit intent, and runtime change. Their environments are either live but hard to reproduce, or reproducible but reduced to endpoint-level stubs that remove sessions, artifacts, state transitions, and downstream side effects. We introduce LiveClawBench, a benchmark designed around this dual-fidelity requirement. LiveClawBench combines a Triple-Axis Complexity Framework for difficulty-driven task construction with reproducible full-stack mock applications that preserve stateful execution semantics. With 134 executable cases across 10 domains with 22 mocked services, LiveClawBench supports controlled, extensible, and factor-level diagnostic evaluation of realistic agentic tasks. We release the benchmark resources: (1) Benchmark: https://github.com/Mosi-AI/LiveClawBench; (2) Leaderboard: https://mosi-ai.github.io/LiveClawBench/leaderboard/; (3) Trajectories: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mosi-AI/LiveClawbench-trajectories

items.title: Researchers propose Embedded Language Flows, a continuous diffusion model in embedding space that outperforms discrete and continuous diffusion language models with fewer sampling steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ELF: Embedded Language Flows
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Embedded Language Flows (ELF), a new class of continuous diffusion models for language generation that operate primarily in continuous embedding space before mapping to discrete tokens at the final step. This approach, based on continuous-time Flow Matching, allows ELF to leverage techniques from image-domain diffusion models and achieve superior generation quality with fewer sampling steps compared to existing discrete and continuous diffusion language models.

ELF's design minimizes adaptations needed for discrete language data, enabling effective continuous diffusion modeling in language tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that ELF outperforms leading diffusion language models, suggesting it as a promising direction for advancing continuous diffusion approaches in natural language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.10938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have become the de facto approaches for generating continuous data, e.g., in domains such as images and videos. Their success has attracted growing interest in applying them to language modeling. Unlike their image-domain counterparts, today's leading diffusion language models (DLMs) primarily operate over discrete tokens. In this paper, we show that continuous DLMs can be made effective with minimal adaptation to the discrete domain. We propose Embedded Language Flows (ELF), a class of diffusion models in continuous embedding space based on continuous-time Flow Matching. Unlike existing DLMs, ELF predominantly stays within the continuous embedding space until the final time step, where it maps to discrete tokens using a shared-weight network. This formulation makes it straightforward to adapt established techniques from image-domain diffusion models, e.g., classifier-free guidance (CFG). Experiments show that ELF substantially outperforms leading discrete and continuous DLMs, achieving better generation quality with fewer sampling steps. These results suggest that ELF offers a promising path toward effective continuous DLMs.

items.title: Researchers propose Student-Centric Answer Sampling to improve LLM training by selecting teacher answers based on student learning cost rather than teacher strength alone [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Strongest Teacher Is Not Always the Best Teacher: Student-Centric Answer Selection
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Student-Centric Answer Sampling (SCAS), a new approach to training large language models (LLMs) that selects teacher-generated answers based on the estimated learning cost for the student rather than relying solely on the teacher's overall performance. This method challenges the common practice of using the highest-performing teacher as the best source of supervision, demonstrating that the strongest teacher's answers are not always the most effective for every student model.

SCAS uses a token-wise gradient decomposition to estimate a student-centric learning cost and guides answer selection during training accordingly. Experiments involving 30 teacher models, 6 student models, and 6 tasks showed that SCAS consistently improves student performance, suggesting that tailoring supervision to the student's current state can enhance the effectiveness of knowledge distillation in LLM training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.26872v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM training increasingly relies on teacher-generated supervision, from synthetic responses to reasoning traces and tool-use demonstrations. Current practice often chooses the highest-performing teacher to generate student training data, implicitly treating teacher test performance as a proxy for teaching quality. We show that this assumption can fail: even when multiple teachers provide correct answers to the same question, the answer from the strongest teacher is not necessarily the best supervision for a given student. Experiments across 30 teacher models, 6 student base models, and 6 tasks show that SCAS consistently improves student performance, suggesting that effective distillation should prioritize supervision matched to the current student rather than teacher strength alone.

items.title: Reference MCP launches tool enabling AI agents to search each other's past sessions across multiple platforms locally and offline [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Reference MCP – let your AI agents search each other's past sessions
items.summary:
Reference MCP is a local, offline tool that allows AI agents to search and access each other's past session transcripts and memory files across multiple platforms. By integrating with tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Cursor, it enables seamless cross-tool collaboration and information retrieval without data leaving the user's machine.

The tool operates through a single MCP server that reads session data from various AI tools on the user's device, using a lightweight BM25 ranking system for efficient search. It supports easy setup with minimal dependencies and is extensible to additional tools via simple configuration, enhancing AI agents' ability to recall and reference previous interactions across different environments.

items.originalTitle: Weathering the Storm of AI
items.summary:
The article explores the challenges and opportunities brought by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, emphasizing the importance of ethical considerations and skill development. It advises professionals to navigate AI's evolving landscape thoughtfully, avoiding burnout and maintaining critical thinking rather than relying solely on AI tools. The author highlights that no one has fully mastered AI yet, and cautions against blaming AI for broader industry issues, encouraging users to leverage AI to enhance their abilities rather than outsource their expertise.

The discussion includes practical perspectives on how to engage with AI constructively, such as questioning AI decisions and using it as a collaborative partner to accelerate learning. The article underscores the need for a balanced approach to AI adoption amid ongoing technological change, suggesting that those who actively own their learning process will be better positioned for future success despite uncertainties in the market.

items.originalTitle: Five Forecasts for the Future of Work
items.summary:
The article presents five key forecasts about the future of work, emphasizing a fundamental shift driven by AI delegation, command literacy, and changes in labor structures. It argues that work itself—not just jobs—is being transformed as AI becomes more capable and integrated, shifting from a tool for information retrieval to an agent for task execution. This transition redefines how humans interact with AI, moving from asking questions to assigning work orders, which will reshape organizational practices and labor economics.

The forecasts highlight that the traditional model of scaling work by increasing headcount will evolve as AI agents take on substantial work blocks. The article stresses the importance of new skills such as command literacy, delegation, and objective-setting, which will become critical for workers to effectively manage AI-driven labor. This shift is expected to impact various sectors beyond software, including finance, law, sales, and marketing, signaling a broad restructuring of how work is organized and measured in the future.

items.title: Researchers introduce ODYSSEY, a categorical framework for constructing verifiable local truth-preserving foundation models using composable foundries, with full implementation and testing across diverse domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Odyssey: Constructing Verifiable Local Truth-Preserving Foundation Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ODYSSEY, a categorical framework designed to construct verifiable, local truth-preserving foundation models through compositions of modular components called foundries. These foundries organize knowledge with built-in argumentation and cover various domains such as evidence, decision-making, finance, and scientific research. The framework employs Universal Foundry Learning to formalize foundry construction using advanced mathematical tools, and Foundry SQL to query and integrate external models securely.

ODYSSEY has been fully implemented and tested across diverse concrete foundries, demonstrating its capability to support domain construction, artifact management, diagnostic analysis, and causal claim extraction from heterogeneous sources. This comprehensive approach ensures robust verification and local truth preservation in foundation models. The research will be presented as a tutorial at ICML 2026, highlighting its significance for advancing trustworthy AI model development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a categorical framework called ODYSSEY for constructing verifiable, local truth-preserving foundation models as compositions of foundries: building-block architectural components that specify a cover of local contexts, local representation families, restriction maps, gluing rules, obstruction policies, update obligations, and human-facing views. A foundry is an organized sheaf of knowledge that carries within it an argumentation component. Concrete foundries are built from generic foundries such as evidence/argument, operational decision, institutional/financial, market meaning, scientific challenge, research-program, assistant-build, and evaluation-harness foundries. Universal Foundry Learning (UFL) formalizes foundry construction as a composition of left and right Kan extensions, with left Kan extension rolling local artifacts into candidate foundries and right Kan extension enforcing the restriction, gluing, obstruction, and argumentation conditions required for promotion. Foundry SQL (FSQL) is a small typed query surface for slicing maintained foundry artifacts that uses TICKET (Topos Integration using Causal Kan Extension Transformers) certification for admitting external or pre-built models into durable ODYSSEY state. ODYSSEY is fully implemented and tested across a wide spectrum of concrete foundries, showing that the same categorical machinery supports domain construction, artifact replay, sheaf diagnostics, grounded Toulmin/local-LLM scrutiny, residual-obstruction ledgers, and optimized TICKET-compatible causal-claim extraction across heterogeneous sources. This paper is to be presented as a 2.5 hour tutorial at ICML 2026. The tutorial home page is at https://bit.ly/4ajS0nA.

items.title: Researchers propose SD-GPS, a solver-driven framework combining autoformalization and verified theorem proposing to improve geometry problem solving with neuro-symbolic methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Verifiable Geometry Problem Solving: Solver-Driven Autoformalization and Theorem Proposing
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SD-GPS, a solver-driven framework designed to enhance geometry problem solving by integrating neural and symbolic methods. This approach addresses key limitations in current systems by linking the symbolic solver directly to both the autoformalization and theorem proving stages, improving compatibility and overcoming deductive impasses. SD-GPS combines supervised learning and reinforcement learning for formal language adaptation and employs an impasse-aware agent to propose verified auxiliary lemmas, ensuring soundness through symbolic verification.

Evaluations on benchmark datasets Geometry3K and PGPS9K show that SD-GPS outperforms existing large language models and neuro-symbolic methods across various problem-solving tasks. By closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution, this framework significantly advances geometric reasoning and demonstrates how neural agents can be grounded in formal systems to achieve verifiable and effective problem-solving capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometry Problem Solving have increasingly adopt the neuro-symbolic paradigm, combining neural intuition with symbolic rigor. However, current frameworks suffer from severe bottlenecks in two core stages: autoformalization, which treats multimodal translation as a static task decoupled from downstream solver compatibility, and theorem prediction, where solvers frequently hit a deductive impasse due to fixed rule libraries. To address these, we propose SD-GPS, a solver-driven framework that treats the symbolic solver as an execution oracle throughout both formalization and deduction. First, Solver-Driven Autoformalization unifies supervised formal-language adaptation and solvability-guided reinforcement learning into a single module built on QwenVL3-2B, making executability the central training signal. Second, Verified Theorem Proposing introduces an impasse-aware agent that proposes local auxiliary lemmas from current proof states, ensuring soundness by filtering all proposals through symbolic verification. Empirical evaluations on Geometry3K and PGPS9K demonstrate that SD-GPS consistently outperforms existing MLLM, neural, and neuro-symbolic methods across standard completion, multiple-choice, and cross-modal reference regimes, proving that closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution significantly improves geometric reasoning, offering profound insights into how neural agents can be grounded by formal systems to achieve verifiable problem-solving capabilities.

items.title: Researchers introduce Lifted Causal Inference algorithm using parametric causal factor graphs to speed up causal effect computation in relational domains with partial causal knowledge support [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lifted Causal Inference
items.summary: Researchers have developed the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm, which uses parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) to efficiently compute causal effects in relational domains. This approach leverages lifted inference to speed up causal effect computation by representing indistinguishable objects collectively, maintaining exact results while improving performance compared to traditional propositional methods like causal Bayesian networks. The team also introduced partially directed PCFGs (PD-PCFGs) to handle scenarios with partial causal knowledge, broadening the applicability of lifted causal inference to models with less prior causal information.
items.description: Researchers have developed the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm, which uses parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) to efficiently compute causal effects in relational domains. This approach leverages lifted inference to speed up causal effect computation by representing indistinguishable objects collectively, maintaining exact results while improving performance compared to traditional propositional methods like causal Bayesian networks. The team also introduced partially directed PCFGs (PD-PCFGs) to handle scenarios with partial causal knowledge, broadening the applicability of lifted causal inference to models with less prior causal information.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lifted inference exploits indistinguishabilities in probabilistic graphical models by using a representative for indistinguishable objects, thereby speeding up query answering while maintaining exact answers. In this article, we show how lifting can be applied to efficiently compute causal effects in relational domains. More specifically, we introduce parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) to incorporate causal knowledge in lifted models and give a formal semantics of interventions therein. We further present the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm to compute causal effects on a lifted level, thereby drastically speeding up causal inference compared to propositional inference, e.g., in causal Bayesian networks. In addition, we present partially directed parametric causal factor graphs (PD-PCFGs) as a generalisation of PCFGs to handle partial causal knowledge and extend LCI to perform lifted causal inference in a PD-PCFG, thereby extending the applicability of lifted causal inference to a broader range of models requiring less prior knowledge about causal relationships.

items.title: Researchers propose OverFlowLight, a real-time traffic signal control framework that reduces urban intersection gridlock by 60.4% and increases throughput by 18.2% across 43 intersections in three cities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OverFlowLight: Real-Time Gridlock Prevention and Traffic Signal Optimization for Urban Intersections
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OverFlowLight, a real-time traffic signal control framework designed to prevent gridlock at urban intersections by addressing queue overflow, a common cause of severe congestion. Tested across 43 intersections in three cities, OverFlowLight reduces overflow incidents by 60.4% and increases traffic throughput by 18.2% compared to existing systems. The framework uses multi-modal sensing from cameras and radars to detect overflow and dynamically adjusts signal phases to clear blocked queues, combining rapid rule-based interventions with reinforcement learning for improved efficiency.

The system integrates seamlessly with current reinforcement learning-based traffic controllers, demonstrating modularity and practical applicability. By significantly reducing the need for manual adjustments typical of expert-tuned signal plans, OverFlowLight offers a scalable, data-driven solution to enhance urban traffic management and prevent cascading gridlocks, contributing to more resilient and efficient transportation networks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Queue overflow, a severe consequence of urban traffic congestion, occurs when vehicle queues exceed intersection capacity, obstructing upstream traffic and triggering cascading gridlocks. Prevailing traffic signal control (TSC) algorithms, primarily optimized for throughput, often fail to address overflow during peak hours, exacerbating congestion and creating safety hazards. We propose OverFlowLight, a real-time framework designed to preemptively resolve overflow and enhance overall TSC performance. It first introduces a mechanism to accurately detect overflow in real-time by leveraging multi-modal sensing from cameras and radars. Upon detection, it dynamically generates and inserts dedicated overflow phases into the signal cycle to clear the blocking queues. This is orchestrated by a hybrid control design that combines rapid rule-based overflow intervention with controller back ends such as reinforcement learning (RL) for longer-horizon efficiency. We conducted extensive real-world deployments of OverFlowLight across 43 intersections in three major cities. The framework demonstrates seamless integration with existing RL-based TSC agents, highlighting its modularity and practical applicability. Empirical results show that OverFlowLight reduces overflow incidents by 60.4% and increases network throughput by 18.2% compared to deployed baselines. Furthermore, it substantially diminishes the need for manual intervention common with expert-tuned signal plans. This work presents the first practical, scalable, and data-driven framework for actively preventing traffic gridlock, offering a crucial component for building resilient and efficient urban transportation systems. Our demonstration videos, codes and datasets are available at the anonymous URL, https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OverFlowLight-FBF9.

items.title: Researchers release CalBrief, a pilot benchmark evaluating large language models' ability to generate evidence-calibrated scientific briefings across 16 evidence packages and 96 verified takeaways [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CalBrief: A Pilot Diagnostic Benchmark for Evidence-Calibrated Scientific Briefing with Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CalBrief, a pilot benchmark designed to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) ability to generate scientific briefings that accurately reflect the strength and scope of supporting evidence. The benchmark includes 16 diverse scientific evidence packages and 96 human-verified takeaways, using an auditable framework to identify where LLMs struggle in evidence calibration. The study found that while structured organization improves reasoning about roles and gaps in evidence, explicit strength-calibration policies tend to be overly conservative compared to baseline models.

The research involved testing three closed-model backbones—GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, and Gemini Flash—to diagnose causes of conservatism in strength calibration. Results showed that expanding the label space from binary to a four-way classification accounted for most of the conservatism, while other factors had minimal impact. Additionally, the study revealed that four-way predictions could be simplified back to binary labels without loss of information, indicating that nuanced labels carry valuable insights. The findings highlight a tension between label-level strength judgment and auditable evidence organization, suggesting these capabilities should be evaluated separately in LLM research assistants.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as research assistants, yet it remains unclear whether they can calibrate research takeaways to the strength and scope of the supporting evidence. We study evidence-calibrated scientific briefing: given a bounded package of related papers, a system should generate package-level takeaways with evidence strength, scope boundaries, and missing-evidence caveats. We contribute a verified pilot benchmark of 16 heterogeneous scientific evidence packages and 96 human-verified takeaways, and we use CalBrief, an auditable role/gap/strength framework, as a diagnostic probe to locate where briefing breaks down. Under a fair-schema evaluation, structured organization improves role and gap reasoning, but an explicit strength-calibration policy is systematically over-conservative and falls below majority and direct-LLM baselines. To explain why, we run a controlled diagnostic across three closed-model backbones (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Gemini Flash) that separates three potential causes of conservatism. Approximately 63% of the conservatism gap is attributable to expanding the label space from binary {moderate, weak} to four-way {moderate, weak, uncertain, insufficient_evidence} (p < 0.001 across all backbones); only 1% is attributable to gap/scope signal injection (not significant); the remaining 36% arises from the pipeline policy itself. We also find that 4-way predictions can be post-hoc collapsed back to binary and then match or exceed direct binary prompting, so the extra labels carry information that strict matching hides. Label-level strength judgment and auditable evidence organization are distinct abilities currently in tension, and should be evaluated separately for LLM research assistants.

items.title: Researchers introduce DMV-Bench, the first interactive benchmark for multimodal agent visual memory using incidental cue injection in a 1,000-product e-commerce catalog [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DMV-Bench: Diagnosing Long-Horizon Multimodal Agents' Visual Memory with Incidental Cue Injection
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DMV-Bench, the first interactive benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal agents' visual memory in an environment where agents must recall visual information rather than relying on text. Built on a controlled e-commerce catalog of 1,000 home-furnishing products, DMV-Bench uses unique incidental visual cues embedded in product images to test an agent's ability to remember and navigate to specific items across multiple autonomous shopping sessions. The benchmark ensures that discriminative signals come solely from visual data, preventing text leakage.

The team also proposed DualMem, a novel memory architecture inspired by dual-coding theory, which maintains parallel visual and verbal codes. DualMem outperformed existing multimodal agent-memory systems and a caption-based baseline across various task lengths on two different models, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The approach emphasizes visual cues for end-to-end memory while using verbal channels primarily for query grounding, demonstrating improved performance in long-horizon visual memory tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Research on agent memory has matured rapidly, but almost entirely on the text side: few existing benchmarks ask, in an interactive environment, when an agent genuinely needs to remember what it saw rather than what it could write down. We introduce DMV-Bench (Code: https://github.com/yyyujintang/DMV-Bench), the first interactive benchmark for multimodal-agent visual memory. DMV-Bench is built on a controlled home-furnishing e-commerce catalogue of 1,000 product variants in which a text-leakage contract keeps the discriminative signal of each task in the pixels alone. Across a chain of autonomous shopping sessions, every visited product image carries a unique, pre-rendered incidental cue, and the agent is later asked to recall a particular cued product and navigate to its URL. Inspired by dual-coding theory, we propose DualMem, a memory architecture that maintains a visual and a verbal code in parallel. On DMV-Bench, DualMem outperforms a caption baseline and three recent multimodal agent-memory systems at every chain length J in {5, 10, 15, 50} on both Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, with the lead surviving controls for memory-bank size and encoding-position bias, and an asymmetric dual-coding regime in which vision carries the cue end-to-end while the verbal channel plays a smaller query-grounding role.

items.title: Researchers propose LaViD framework transferring semantic knowledge from language-only large models to vision-only models, outperforming recent multimodal distillation methods on fine-grained benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Large Language Model Teaches Visual Students: Cross-Modality Transfer of Fine-Grained Conceptual Knowledge
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LaViD, a framework that transfers semantic knowledge from large language models (LLMs) to vision-only models without relying on paired multimodal data. LaViD uses LLMs to generate multiple-choice questions that capture semantic distinctions between visual classes, creating soft label distributions that guide the vision model through an auxiliary distillation loss. This approach enables a language-only teacher model to effectively supervise a visual student model.

LaViD outperforms recent multimodal distillation methods like MaKD and achieves competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art visual distillation techniques such as DKD and MLKD across multiple fine-grained benchmarks. It also enhances robustness to spurious correlations, as demonstrated by improved worst-group accuracy on the Waterbirds dataset. The framework's code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27527v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) possess broad conceptual knowledge acquired through large-scale text pretraining, yet their potential to supervise models in other modalities remains underexplored. In this work, we propose LaViD--Language-to-Visual Knowledge Distillation--a simple and effective framework for transferring high-level semantic knowledge from a language-only teacher to a vision-only student model. Instead of relying on paired multimodal data, LaViD elicits conceptual signals from an LLM by prompting it to generate multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that probe semantic distinctions between visual classes. Each class is mapped to a soft label distribution over these MCQs, forming a rich conceptual signature that guides the student through an auxiliary distillation loss. Notably, despite using a language-only teacher without access to image data, LaViD consistently outperforms recent methods like MaKD that distill from vision-language models across multiple fine-grained benchmarks. It also achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art visual distillation methods such as DKD and MLKD, with further gains when combined with logit standardization. On the Waterbirds dataset, LaViD substantially improves worst-group accuracy, demonstrating enhanced robustness to spurious correlations with distillation. Code is available at https://github.com/lliangthomas/lavid.

items.title: Researchers introduce the context-ready transformer, a recurrent neural network architecture that pre-contextualizes tokens for faster generation and improved performance over standard transformers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Context-Ready Transformer
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the context-ready transformer, a novel recurrent neural network architecture that enhances token processing by pre-contextualizing each token before it enters a transformer block. This approach uses a correction network to combine previous context with the current token embedding, enabling faster and more efficient left-to-right generation. The model can be trained by unrolling the correction process and can also be adapted from pretrained transformers through fine-tuning.

Evaluations show that a five-layer context-ready transformer outperforms a 12-layer standard transformer while generating text 1.7 times faster on an A100 GPU. A single-layer version achieves a 2.6 times speedup over a six-layer transformer, with comparable performance in terms of perplexity. The architecture is particularly effective with wide representations and long contexts, and it demonstrates superior compositional abilities on tasks like pointer-chasing compared to standard transformers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the context-ready transformer, a new recurrent neural network architecture built from a D-layer transformer block that pre-contextualizes each token before it enters the block. During left-to-right generation, a correction network combines the previous position's block output -- a cached summary of past context -- with the current token embedding, so the tokenenters the block already contextualized rather than as a raw embedding. At sequential inference, the correction chain makes the architecture a recurrent neural network. For training, we unroll the correction process K times over the full sequence, processing all positions in parallel at each step. A pretrained transformer can also be converted to a context-ready model by adding a zero-initialized correction FFN and fine-tuning. We evaluate across widths, depths, block sizes, and two datasets, with all comparisons against standard transformers, variants, and ablations. A D=5 model beats a 12-layer transformer while generating 1.7x faster on an A100. With K=10, a single-layermodel (D=1) beats a 6-layer transformer with a 2.6x inference speedup, and sequential inference matches parallel K=10 to within 0.01 PPL. The architecture benefits most from wide representations and long contexts. On a pointer-chasing task, D=1 trained with BPTT solves all 10 composition levels, while standard transformers exhibit staircase-like depth dependence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Social media popularity prediction aims to forecast the future reach or influence of online content from early-stage observations. Accurate prediction enables key downstream applications, such as advertising optimization and strategic content planning by users, creators, and platforms. Despite substantial progress, existing popularity prediction works often fail to jointly consider multimodal content and temporal social interaction signals. Moreover, the literature remains highly fragmented across datasets, modalities, observation windows, prediction targets, and evaluation protocols. This fragmentation prevents fair comparison and obscures a systematic understanding of how textual, visual, temporal, and interaction-based signals jointly shape popularity dynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce MMG-Pop, a Multi-modal Graph-based Popularity Prediction benchmark, which unifies datasets, modalities, temporal interaction signals, and representative baselines under a standardized evaluation protocol. Furthermore, we propose MMG-PopNet, a unified multi-modal graph-based network that jointly models the aforementioned multi-modal signals and graph-structured social interactions. Extensive experiments on MMG-Pop, comprising four datasets across Bluesky and Reddit platforms, demonstrate the superior performance of MMG-PopNet and yield new insights into cross-platform training generalization, multi-task prediction benefits, multi-modality contributions, and LLM prediction limitation. These findings establish a unified foundation for future research on social dynamics modeling and intervention under heterogeneous modalities and socially-aware agentic ecosystem paradigms.

items.title: Researchers prove perfect prompt-injection prevention is mathematically impossible in shared-embedding sequence models without architectural separation of instructions and data [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Inseparability of Instructions and Data in Shared-Embedding Sequence Models
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that perfect prevention of prompt injection attacks in large language model (LLM) applications is mathematically impossible within shared-embedding sequence models that do not separate instructions from data. Their study formalizes these systems as Prompted Action Models and introduces the concept of Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC), which requires system behavior to depend solely on the meaning of untrusted input rather than its encoding. They prove that achieving SFC is unattainable due to inherent inseparability of trusted and untrusted content, exposure of control paths to untrusted tokens, and limitations of finite training data.

The findings highlight structural vulnerabilities in current shared-embedding architectures, drawing parallels to longstanding security issues like buffer overflows in traditional computing. The researchers argue that no in-pipeline classification or alignment method alone can fully eliminate prompt injection risks. Instead, they conclude that architectural changes enforcing a clear separation between instruction and data channels are necessary to address this fundamental security challenge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prompt injection is the top security risk for LLM-integrated applications, yet every defense proposed so far has been broken. We prove this is not a coincidence: in shared-embedding architectures that lack enforced control-data separation, perfect prompt-injection prevention is mathematically impossible. We formalize prompted systems as Prompted Action Models whose outputs include control-authoritative actions: refusal decisions, tool authorization, policy routing, and memory writes. We define Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC), the property that such behavior depends only on the meaning of untrusted input, not on how it is encoded. We then prove SFC is unachievable within the shared pipeline, via three results: a provenance-recovery impossibility (shared representations make trusted and untrusted content statistically inseparable, bounded by total variation distance); control-path exposure (untrusted tokens enter control-relevant computation through the same attention value-aggregation that determines outputs); and a finite-coverage invariance gap (finite training cannot certify invariance over infinite semantic-equivalence classes). We ground each quantity in measurements on production tokenizers and models. The result is structural, not a gap in current defenses. It mirrors the code-data confusion in Von Neumann machines that gives rise to buffer overflows, a vulnerability class that took decades of layered defenses (DEP, Write-XOR-Execute, ASLR, stack canaries, and ultimately memory-safe languages) to contain, because no single mechanism sufficed. The implication is the same: prompt injection cannot be eliminated by better in-pipeline classification or alignment alone. It requires architectural separation of instruction and data channels. We identify the root cause and the class of solution it demands.

items.title: Researchers propose HIA-GAT, a heterogeneous graph attention network for frame-level traffic conflict risk prediction on freeways, achieving top risk-ranking performance on NGSIM I-80 and US-101 datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: hia-gat: A Heterogeneous Interaction-Aware Graph Attention Network For Frame-Level Traffic Conflict Risk Prediction On Freeways
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HIA-GAT, a heterogeneous graph attention network designed for frame-level traffic conflict risk prediction on freeways. This model treats risk assessment as a multi-agent scene graph classification task, using vehicles as nodes and modeling interactions through longitudinal and lateral edges enriched with physics-informed features. Tested on the NGSIM I-80 and US-101 datasets, HIA-GAT outperformed existing models in risk-ranking accuracy, particularly excelling in scenarios involving lane-change conflicts where relational structure is crucial.

HIA-GAT employs a dual-stream attention mechanism to separately process longitudinal and lateral interactions, integrating them via a conflict-type-aware gating system supervised by conflict attribution data. This approach not only improves prediction accuracy but also offers interpretable insights into dominant conflict types per vehicle, enabling real-time, actionable freeway safety monitoring. The study highlights the importance of graph structures for modeling lateral conflict risks, while longitudinal risks can often be captured without relational modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper formulates frame-level freeway risk assessment as a multi-agent scene graph-level binary classification problem, where each video or trajectory frame is labeled risky if any TTC- or PET-based conflict violates a specified severity threshold. We construct a relation-aware graph per frame with vehicles as nodes and two interaction types as edges: same-lane (longitudinal) and adjacent-lane (lateral), augmented with physics-informed edge features aligned to rear-end and lane-change conflict mechanisms. Building on a structured benchmarking suite of non-graph models and graph baselines, we propose HIA-GAT, a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network that processes longitudinal and lateral interactions through dedicated attention pathways and fuses them via a conflict-type-aware gating mechanism with event-level gate supervision derived from SSM conflict attribution. Experiments on the NGSIM I-80 and US-101 freeway datasets across nine TTC and PET threshold configurations show that HIA-GAT achieves the best average risk-ranking performance (AUC 0.835 on I-80 and 0.867 on US-101), with the largest gains on PET-only (lane-change) settings where relational structure is essential. Beyond accuracy, the learned gate provides interpretable per-vehicle attribution of dominant conflict type, supporting actionable, real-time freeway safety monitoring. We show that graph structure is critical for modeling lateral conflict risk, while longitudinal risk can often be captured by non-relational aggregation.

items.title: Researchers propose PEBS, a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage method for RLHF reward-model calibration that reduces RMSE by up to 9.66% without retraining the base model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PEBS: Per-rater Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage for RLHF Reward-Model Calibration
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PEBS, a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage method designed to improve reward-model calibration in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Unlike traditional approaches that use a single global calibrator for all annotators, PEBS fits individual affine calibrators for each rater and applies empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean without retraining the base reward model. This method significantly reduces root mean square error (RMSE) by up to 9.66% on benchmark datasets, enhancing the accuracy of reward models by better accounting for individual annotator differences.

PEBS operates as a closed-form, post-hoc estimator that adjusts annotator-specific calibration maps at inference time, leaving the underlying reward model unchanged. The approach was tested on the PRISM and PluriHarms datasets, demonstrating consistent RMSE improvements over the standard pooled population-slope baseline. This advancement offers a practical way to refine RLHF reward models by addressing systematic rating-scale variations among annotators, potentially leading to more reliable human feedback integration in reinforcement learning systems.
