items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward models for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pool preferences across thousands of annotators and fit one global affine calibrator, collapsing raters with systematically different rating-scale offsets and slopes into a single average-rater fit that does not match any individual annotator. PEBS is a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator: it fits per-rater affine calibrators on a held-out slice of each annotator's ratings and applies Morris-James-Stein empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean, in closed form and without retraining the reward model. On PRISM, PEBS reduces within-user held-out RMSE by 8.58% over the pooled population-slope baseline. The procedure replicates on PluriHarms harm ratings (Qwen-2.5 base, in-family) with a +9.66% RMSE reduction over the same population-slope baseline. PEBS is a closed-form post-hoc estimator for annotator-specific affine calibration in RLHF reward modeling; it leaves the reward base model unchanged and estimates only the rater-level map used at inference time for new ratings.

items.title: Researchers develop distribution-based deep multiple instance learning model for tumor proportion scoring in non-small cell lung cancer using slide-level labels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Distribution-based deep multiple instance learning for tumor proportion scoring in NSCLC
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a novel deep multiple instance learning (MIL) model to improve tumor proportion scoring (TPS) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using only slide-level labels. The approach combines an embedding-extraction and multiclass-classification network to capture histopathological features of tissue patches with a MIL model that predicts zero-inflated beta (ZIBeta) parameters representing the TPS probability distribution for entire slides. This distribution-based framework enhances prediction accuracy and explainability compared to traditional methods.

The model addresses challenges such as the labor-intensive manual annotation of slides and the scarcity of certified experts by leveraging slide-level TPS scores without requiring detailed patch annotations. The ZIBeta modeling significantly outperforms baseline linear and ridge regression techniques, effectively handling non-expressive images and capturing expected accuracy through distribution concentration, demonstrating its potential for aiding treatment planning and prognosis in NSCLC.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate assessment of tumor proportion score (TPS) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is critical for treatment planning and prognosis. Key challenges include the tedious manual work required to annotate each slide, combined with the limited number of experts certified for this task. Multiple instance learning (MIL) has proven to be an effective approach for predicting TPS scores at the slide level; however, existing methods struggle with non-expressive (zero class) images. Our approach involves two models: (1) an embedding-extraction and multiclass-classification network that captures the histopathological features of individual patches, and (2) a MIL model that aggregates these embeddings to predict zero-inflated beta (ZIBeta) parameters representing the overall TPS probability distribution for the entire slide. Using only slide-level TPS scores as labels, we demonstrate how this end-to-end framework can leverage a novel distribution-based architecture to improve prediction accuracy and explainability. ZIBeta modeling significantly outperforms baseline linear and ridge regression while capturing expected accuracy through distribution concentration.

items.title: Researchers introduce Retroactive Advantage Correction to reduce bias in delay-aware reinforcement learning from human feedback, improving policy accuracy by up to 47.9x in tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Retroactive Advantage Correction: Closed-Form V-Trace Bias Correction for Delay-Aware RLHF
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC), a method designed to address delays in reward signals during reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). This approach queues and adjusts delayed feedback, reinjecting it into the learning process to correct bias caused by asynchronous rewards. Tests on a tabular Markov decision process showed that RAC can reduce policy bias by up to 47.9 times compared to existing methods, while also lowering computational costs.

RAC works by applying a non-negative kernel to age pending feedback and reintegrate it as a clipped residual in subsequent optimization steps. The method is mathematically proven to be unbiased when all delayed feedback is accounted for and generalizes existing techniques like V-trace in the absence of delay. It integrates easily with popular reinforcement learning algorithms such as PPO and GRPO through minimal code changes.

This advancement improves the accuracy and efficiency of RLHF systems that rely on slow or queued human or automated feedback, potentially enhancing the performance of AI models trained in real-world environments where immediate reward signals are not always available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in production does not always have a synchronous reward signal. Code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, and queued human review can return several gradient steps after the rollout that produced them, breaking the synchronous-reward assumption underlying standard PPO. We address this gap with Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC): each pending slow completion is queued, aged through a non-negative kernel, and reinjected as a clipped residual into the next optimiser step's advantage. We prove that under an unbiased clipped importance ratio, the cumulative RAC correction is exactly unbiased when the effective delay kernel reinjects all of its mass, and carries a bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise; at the no-delay identity kernel it reduces to V-trace. On a tabular Markov decision process (MDP) proof-of-concept, RAC reduces the closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9x at the two-slow-channel configuration, beating wait-for-slow at lower wall-clock cost. RAC integrates with PPO and GRPO through a two-line reward-manager patch.

items.title: Researchers present Narrative-UFET, a method generating short narratives to improve ultra-fine entity typing on long-tail types by leveraging multi-sentence context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Narrative-UFET: Narrative Generation for Ultra-Fine Entity Typing
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Narrative-UFET, a novel approach to ultra-fine entity typing (UFET) that generates short, coherent narratives to provide multi-sentence context for entity mentions. This method addresses the challenge of accurately typing long-tail entities, which traditional sentence-level UFET methods struggle with due to limited contextual information. By pairing each entity with an automatically generated narrative, the researchers demonstrate improved performance, especially when the entity's type changes within the narrative, highlighting the value of extended discourse context.

The study compares two narrative variants: one maintaining a constant entity type and another allowing type shifts, with the latter yielding stronger improvements over sentence-level baselines. Additionally, synthetic narratives outperform naturally occurring contexts, suggesting that controlled narrative construction can reveal implicit signals missed in real text. Despite these advances, the findings indicate significant opportunities for further research in discourse modeling and narrative generation to enhance entity typing accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultra-fine entity typing (UFET) assigns highly specific types to entity mentions, but current approaches struggle with types in the long tail. We hypothesize that a key limitation is the reliance on sentence-level context, since disambiguating evidence is often spread across multiple sentences. Testing this has been difficult because all existing UFET resources are sentence-level. We present Narrative-UFET, a controlled extension of UFET in which each entity mention is paired with an automatically generated short, coherent narrative. Synthesizing narratives lets us isolate the effect of specific discourse properties. We experiment with two paired variants: one in which the entity's type is held constant across the narrative (Maintain) and one in which it shifts (Change). We show that narrative context yields consistent improvements on long-tail types over sentence-level baselines, with the Change variant providing the stronger signal. A comparison against naturally occurring contexts shows that synthetic narratives yield stronger gains, indicating that controlled discourse construction can surface signals that real text leaves implicit. Substantial room for improvement remains, suggesting open directions in both discourse modeling and narrative construction.

items.title: Researchers introduce KARMA, a method using K-order Markov approximations to explain temporal dependencies in multivariate time series forecasting models, validated on real and synthetic data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Global Explanations for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting Models via $K$-Order Markov Approximations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed KARMA, a novel method that uses K-order Markov approximations to explain temporal dependencies in multivariate time series forecasting models. KARMA constructs a Markov surrogate model to capture the temporal relationships learned by the predictor, addressing the common limitation of existing explainable AI methods that assume timestamp features are independent. The approach identifies the minimal history length needed for accurate prediction, estimates the best-fitting Markov transition kernel, and provides a hierarchical global explanation framework, demonstrated on real-world weather data.

The method was validated using complex synthetic data with known causal structures, showing that KARMA can recover the causal dependencies learned by the model more effectively than established attribution techniques like TimeSHAP. This advancement offers a more accurate and interpretable understanding of temporal dependencies in time series forecasting models, which is crucial for applications requiring sequential and causal consistency in explanations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While many explainable AI (XAI) methods have been proposed, most are not designed for time-series forecasting models and often rely on the implicit assumption that timestamp features are independent. This assumption ignores the fundamental property of temporal dependence and can lead to explanations that violate the sequential and causal structure of the data. We introduce \textsc{KARMA}, a method for explaining time-series predictors by constructing a Markov surrogate model that captures the temporal dependencies learned by the predictor. Our approach revolves around three main aspects: identifying the minimal history length $K$ that is predictively sufficient for the model, estimating the best-fitting $K$-order Markov transition kernel from the discretized history space, and a five-level global explanation hierarchy that can be derived from the Markov transition kernel, which we illustrate using real-world weather data (Beijing PM 2.5). We also certify using complex synthetic data with known true causal edges that KARMA (i) recovers the data causal structure as learned by the model via a controlled experiment and (ii) identifies temporal dependencies better than established attribution methods such as TimeSHAP.

items.title: Researchers propose HybridCodec combining discrete tokens and continuous residuals for efficient speech language models, improving speaker characteristic retention and reducing autoregressive steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HybridCodec: Modeling Discrete and Continuous Representations for Efficient Speech Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HybridCodec, a new approach that combines discrete audio tokens with continuous residuals to enhance speech language models. This hybrid framework uses a discrete-continuous focal modulation codec alongside a hybrid Transformer, enabling efficient autoregressive inference in the discrete domain while applying non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. The method improves the preservation of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only models and reduces the number of autoregressive steps needed.

The approach addresses the common issue of information loss during audio discretization, which has previously led to performance degradation in multimodal text-audio systems and large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that HybridCodec effectively balances compression and detail retention, offering a promising direction for integrating audio capabilities into language models with improved efficiency and fidelity.

However, numerous studies report performance degradation on various downstream tasks due to information loss during discretization. To address this, we propose a novel approach combining temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals. Our framework consists of a hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec and a hybrid Transformer. This architecture performs autoregressive inference in the discrete domain, coupled with non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the retention of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only methods, while simultaneously reducing the number of required autoregressive steps.

items.title: Researchers propose dual-threshold hard example mining to improve cross-platform Chinese offensive comment detection, demonstrating significant gains across Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Platform Chinese Offensive Comment Detection via Dual-Threshold Hard Example Mining
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a dual-threshold hard example mining method to improve the detection of offensive comments across multiple Chinese social media platforms, including Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu. This approach addresses the common issue of performance degradation when deploying offensive comment detection models across different platforms by filtering error-prone samples based on prediction confidence and fine-tuning the model with a small set of manually labeled difficult examples. The method demonstrated significant performance improvements compared to baseline models under domain shifts.

The study involved fine-tuning a RoBERTa model on a Chinese offensive language dataset to establish a baseline, followed by constructing a three-class fine-labeled test set spanning four platforms. The researchers quantified domain differences using metrics like Jaccard and Proxy-A Distance and identified bottlenecks in baseline performance. Their dual-threshold strategy selectively mines hard examples from unlabeled data, enabling low-cost cross-platform adaptation and enhancing detection accuracy in diverse social media contexts.

The paper proposes a dual-threshold hard mining method to address this. First, the clean-Chinese-base RoBERTa is finetuned on COLD to establish a binary baseline for fair comparison. Second, a three-class fine-labeled test set covering Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu is constructed, domain distances from the source are quantified using Jaccard and Proxy-A Distance, as well as the degradation bottleneck of the baseline under domain shift is systematically revealed. Herein, a dual threshold hard example mining strategy is proposed. High- and low-confidence error-prone samples are filtered from unlabeled corpora by prediction confidence. The model is secondarily finetuned under implicit contexts with merely a small set of manually labeled hard examples, realizing low-cost cross-platform domain adaptation. Experiments reveal significant performance gains of the optimized model across four platforms.

items.title: Researchers conduct factorised study of probe-based uncertainty estimation in large language models, finding structured features more robust under distribution shift and providing pretrained probes for factual generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Signals to Transfer: A Factorised Study of Probe-Based Uncertainty Estimation in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a detailed study on probe-based uncertainty estimation (UE) methods used to detect hallucinations in large language models (LLMs). Their factorised analysis under controlled conditions reveals that while raw hidden states and attention features perform well within the same data domain, structured and compressed features demonstrate greater robustness when models face distribution shifts. The study also highlights the significant impact of prompting and label construction on probe behavior.

Building on these insights, the team developed pretrained probes based on benchmark data that transfer effectively to open-ended factual generation tasks, offering a reliable baseline for uncertainty estimation. This work emphasizes the need for evaluation approaches that reflect real-world deployment scenarios and provides resources to support further research in this area.

Yet, recent methods vary simultaneously across feature design, training data construction, and evaluation setting, obscuring what actually drives performance. To address this issue, we propose a factorised study of probe-based UE under matched conditions. Our results show that raw hidden states and attention features are difficult to outperform in-domain. However, under distribution shift, structured and compressed features are more robust, suggesting that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to measure progress. Furthermore, prompting and label construction significantly affect probe behaviour. Building on these best-practice findings, we train benchmark-based pretrained probes that transfer reasonably well to open-ended factual generation, providing a stable off-the-shelf baseline. Our work encourages more deployment-oriented evaluation of probe-based uncertainty estimators. The code repository is available at https://github.com/ponhvoan/ProbeUE.

items.originalTitle: CBD: API-Only LLM Black-Box Unlearning through Controlled Behavioral Divergence
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Controlled Behavioral Divergence (CBD), a novel API-only black-box unlearning framework designed for large language models (LLMs). CBD addresses challenges in removing undesired data influence without retraining, especially when only API access is available and when unlearning target data closely resembles retained data. The framework uses auxiliary models to create behavioral divergence and routes unlearning-related prompts away from the target LLM, improving unlearning utility while preserving model performance.

CBD enhances discrimination accuracy by constructing a gradient statistics-based discriminative basis, guiding unlearning signals toward target-specific information rather than shared prompt structures. Compared to eleven existing unlearning methods, CBD demonstrates superior trade-offs between unlearning effectiveness and utility retention, achieving near-retrained reference performance on benchmark tests while maintaining high accuracy on retained knowledge. The code for CBD is publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Edge devices increasingly invoke large language models (LLMs) through API services for context aware edge intelligence, while edge generated data may be collected to improve LLMs and may introduce sensitive, copyrighted, harmful, or outdated information into model behavior. Machine unlearning offers a practical way to remove the influence of undesired data without retraining LLMs. However, existing methods still face two gaps. The first is API only black box access, where target model parameters and internal logits are unavailable. The second is how to preserve retained utility when unlearning target data and retained data share highly similar prompt structures or semantic patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Controlled Behavioral Divergence (CBD), an API only black box unlearning framework. CBD uses two auxiliary models to create controlled behavioral divergence between retained inputs and unlearning target inputs, converts this divergence into an unlearning relevance score, and routes unlearning related prompts away from the target LLM. To improve discrimination accuracy under high similarity between target and retained data, CBD constructs a gradient statistics based discriminative basis by estimating empirical Fisher matrices and solving a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem, guiding the unlearning signal toward target specific information rather than shared prompt structures. Compared with eleven white box and gray box unlearning baselines, CBD achieves a better unlearning utility trade off and its performance varies little across settings. On ToFU forget10, CBD approaches the retrained reference on the forget set while raising model utility to 74.90, about 15% above the second best baseline. On WMDP, it lowers hazardous knowledge accuracy to 25.68, near random guessing, while preserving MMLU accuracy of 52.67. Code is at https://github.com/DGL-codes/CBD.

items.title: Researchers propose preregistration protocol to mitigate p-hacking in LLM-based research by testing on the first eligible future model, blocking transfer of hacks in over 70% of cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mitigating LLM-based p-Hacking by Preregistering for the Next LLM
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a preregistration protocol to reduce p-hacking in studies involving large language models (LLMs). The protocol involves finalizing the experimental procedure on current models, preregistering the analysis plan along with a set of eligible future models, and then conducting the confirmatory analysis on the first eligible LLM released after preregistration. This approach prevents researchers from tuning parameters to achieve desired results on models that do not yet exist, as configurations that exploit one model often do not transfer to subsequent models.

The protocol was tested on two tasks with known true values across 20 models from four providers and 11 analysis configurations. Results showed that it blocked successful transfer of p-hacking in approximately 73% of cases. Additional stress tests confirmed the robustness of the mitigation. The researchers also preregistered their own experiment following the protocol, which confirmed its effectiveness by preventing p-hacking transfer in 6 out of 7 configurations on the first eligible model released after preregistration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, classify, and annotate data whose outputs feed downstream hypothesis tests. However, LLM-based research is easy to p-hack: a researcher can tune the prompts, decoding parameters, or output format until a desired result is reached. We propose a protocol to mitigate p-hacking in LLM-based research: preregistering the experiment and eligible models, and then running it on the first eligible LLM that is released after the preregistration. The researcher finalizes the procedure on current models, preregisters the analysis plan together with a set of eligible future models, and runs the confirmatory analysis on the first eligible model released afterward. Because this model does not exist at commitment time, it cannot be hacked against; furthermore, configurations that hack one model frequently do not transfer to the next. We evaluate the protocol on two tasks whose true values are known. Across 20 models from four providers and 11 LLM-analysis configurations, the protocol would have blocked successful transfer of the p-hack in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases in the two tasks. Additional analyses reveal that mitigation remains substantial under several stress tests. Finally, putting money where our mouth is, we followed our own protocol and preregistered our experiment. The preregistered experiment confirmed the protocol's effectiveness: out of the 7 configurations that hacked the prior model, the hacking failed to carry over in 6 configurations on the first eligible model released afterward.

items.title: Researchers find inference-time rollout rules impact accuracy and cost in multi-horizon volatility forecasting across 20 stock series and multiple model architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Deployment-Side Adaptiveness in Multi-Horizon Volatility Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have found that in multi-horizon volatility forecasting for financial markets, the method used to deploy a trained model at inference time significantly affects both prediction accuracy and computational cost. By experimenting with different rollout rules on 20 stock-volatility series and various model architectures, including linear models and PatchTST, they observed that non-default deployment strategies often outperform the standard multi-output (MIMO) approach. However, the optimal rollout rule varies depending on the model and forecast horizon, making a single fixed strategy unreliable.

To address this variability, the study evaluated validation-based deployment policies that select rollout rules dynamically. These policies improved performance under mean squared error (MSE) objectives while reducing inference costs compared to larger ensembles. The researchers also noted that the effectiveness of deployment policies depends on the evaluation metric, as strategies optimized for MSE did not consistently perform well under QLIKE, a common volatility loss measure in finance. The findings highlight the importance of considering deployment strategies alongside model architecture when assessing volatility forecasting methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In financial forecasting, predictive performance depends not only on which model is trained, but also on how the trained model is deployed. We study this issue in multi-horizon volatility forecasting. Our starting point is that a trained multi-output (MIMO) forecaster does not define a single deployable predictor: by changing the inference-time rollout rule, the same trained model induces a family of forecasts with different accuracy and cost profiles. Across 20 stock-volatility series, three forecast horizons, and architectures ranging from linear models to PatchTST, we find that non-default rollout rules often improve over standard MIMO deployment. However, the best fixed rule varies substantially across architectures and horizons, making any single static replacement unreliable. We therefore evaluate validation-based deployment policies over the induced rule family. Under the primary MSE objective, validation-selected singletons provide a low-cost improvement over default MIMO, while small rule subsets recover much of the benefit of larger ensembles at substantially lower inference cost. We also find that policy rankings are metric-sensitive: MSE-selected policies do not transfer uniformly to QLIKE, a finance-standard volatility loss. These results show that inference-time deployment is a meaningful source of adaptiveness in financial forecasting, and that trained volatility forecasters should be evaluated not only by their architecture, but also by their deployment policy.

items.title: Researchers present a meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that reduces sample complexity 20-fold and enables adaptive compute allocation for real-time neural network certification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Halt Fast! Early Stopping for Certified Robustness
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a meta-learning framework that significantly improves the efficiency of Randomized Smoothing (RS), a method used to provide certified robustness guarantees for neural networks. Their approach reduces the sample complexity by a factor of 20 compared to traditional RS methods while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. This framework uses a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors, enabling adaptive allocation of computational resources during certification.

Unlike standard RS, which requires a fixed and large number of model evaluations per input, this new method supports anytime-valid certification, allowing computation to be adjusted dynamically based on application-specific risk thresholds. This adaptive capability facilitates real-time, safety-critical deployments by enabling resource triage that was previously impossible under classic certification frameworks, all without compromising certification performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized Smoothing (RS) provides rigorous robustness guarantees for neural networks without architectural constraints, yet its adoption is limited by extreme computational costs. Standard RS requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input and forces practitioners to commit to fixed sample sizes a priori. In this work, we present a novel meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that adaptively deploys computational resources. By using a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors for a sequential E-process, we achieve a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to traditional methods while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. Beyond raw efficiency, we demonstrate how anytime-validity enables adaptively allocating compute based upon application-specific risk thresholds, a form of resource triage impossible under classic certification frameworks. That this is achievable while also providing similar certification performance demonstrates that our approach provides a pathway for real-time, safety-critical certification deployments.

items.title: Researchers propose Class-frequency Guided noise schedule for diffusion models to improve generation quality on imbalanced datasets like CIFAR-100-LT and ImageNet-LT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Class-frequency Guided Noise Schedule for Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a Class-frequency Guided (CFRG) noise schedule for diffusion models to enhance generation quality on imbalanced datasets such as CIFAR-100-LT and ImageNet-LT. They identified that low-frequency classes suffer from inaccurately estimated scores due to large low-density regions, which leads to poorer sample quality and diversity compared to high-frequency classes. The CFRG noise schedule addresses this by assigning larger-scale noises to low-frequency classes, improving the balance in score estimation during the diffusion process.

The team tested their approach across tasks including image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation on imbalanced datasets. Their results showed significant improvements over baseline methods, highlighting the importance of incorporating class frequency statistics into the design of noise schedules for score-based generative models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we are the first to examine the correlations between class frequency and the multi-scale noise schedule within diffusion models. For score-based generative models, low-density regions often lead to inaccurately estimated scores, thereby compromising the generation quality. Although the multi-scale noise schedule can alleviate this issue during the diffusion process, low-frequency classes still face the challenge of large low-density regions, resulting in more inaccurate estimated scores than high-frequency classes. Furthermore, high-frequency classes tend to dominate the score space, causing a convergence of most data points towards generating samples from these classes. Consequently, samples generated within low-frequency classes exhibit suboptimal quality and limited diversity. To address this challenge, we propose the \textit{Class-frequency Guided (CFRG)} noise schedule, leveraging the insight that low-frequency classes should be endowed with larger-scale noises. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on various tasks, including image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation, using imbalanced datasets, \textit{i.e.}, CIFAR-100-LT, and ImageNet-LT. By employing the CFRG noise schedule, we achieve substantial improvements over baselines, manifesting the crucial role of frequency statistics in noise schedule design.

items.title: Researchers propose a certification-inspired dual-gate pipeline to reduce word error rate by up to 55% and enhance robustness in automatic speech recognition systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What Was That Again? Certified Robustness for Automatic Speech Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a certification-inspired dual-gate pipeline to improve the robustness of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems, which are typically vulnerable to both adversarial and benign perturbations. This new approach significantly reduces the Word Error Rate (WER) by up to 55%, enhances recall, and lowers the correlation between confidence scores and errors, thereby improving the reliability of ASR outputs without requiring knowledge of the true transcription.

The method involves a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that statistically certifies token existence and excludes adversarial interference, combined with a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the most accurate transcription sequence. Evaluations across four different ASR architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of this pipeline, which also provides detailed word- and sentence-level certifications to strengthen acoustic security and detection capabilities in deployed systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition systems are notoriously both sensitive to adversarial and benign perturbations. While this has been repeatedly demonstrated using reference datasets, detecting such behaviors in deployed systems is incredibly challenging, due to the absence of oracle knowledge of the true transcription. We demonstrate that employing a certification-inspired mechanism can significantly decrease WER, increase recall, and decrease the Spearman correlation between confidence and WER. We achieve this through a dual-gate diagnostic pipeline: a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that accumulates statistical wealth to certify both token existence and adversarial exclusion, and a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning sequence. Our evaluations across four diverse architectures demonstrate up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate, while also providing granular word- and sentence-level certifications to enhance acoustic security.

items.title: Researchers simulate over 8 million over-the-air acoustic attacks, showing up to 94.5% word error rate increase in Whisper and wav2vec voice recognition models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Room for Error: Large-Scale Simulation of Over-the-Air Acoustic Attacks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a high-throughput simulation framework to evaluate over 8 million over-the-air acoustic adversarial attacks on voice recognition models, revealing that such attacks can increase word error rates by up to 94.5% in systems like Whisper and wav2vec. This study addresses previous limitations by incorporating real-world acoustic factors such as detectability and environmental geometry, which were often overlooked in digital-only adversarial testing.

The team introduced a Dual-Form Signal to Noise Ratio metric to separate the stealthiness of the attack source from its effectiveness on the victim system, enabling more precise assessment of attack risks. Their approach lays the foundation for reproducible and verifiable research that fully embraces the complexities of acoustic environments, improving understanding of vulnerabilities in voice-controlled AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While voice control is rapidly becoming a ubiquitous vector of human-AI communication, the risks facing these systems remain poorly understood. This is, in part, a product of the difficulties in scaling strictly digital adversarial workflows to the physical world. These scale barriers have led the community to abstract away key acoustic factors relating to detectability and the influence of geometry on acoustics. These methodological and metrological shortcomings undermine our understanding of risk. We illuminate these issues through real-world testing, conceptual discussions, and a novel, high-throughput reality simulation framework. By testing over 8 million adversarial evaluations, we demonstrate that acoustic awareness yields relative Word Error Rate increases of up to 94.5\% under Whisper and wav2vec. We employ this framework to explore a formalize and operationalize a Dual-Form Signal to Noise Ratio to decouple source stealth from victim attack efficacy, resolving a crucial limitation in current works. This lays the groundwork for repeatable, verifiable research that embraces, rather than abstracts, the acoustic environment.

items.title: Researchers introduce low-agreeableness persona conditioning to reduce jailbreak susceptibility and harmful outputs in large language model fine-tuning while preserving conversational warmth [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Low-Agreeableness Persona Conditioning for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that reduces their vulnerability to jailbreaks and harmful outputs while maintaining conversational warmth. This approach involves conditioning user inputs on a low-agreeableness persona combined with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. Experiments across multiple models demonstrated that this technique lowers harmful output rates compared to traditional warmth fine-tuning methods, which often compromise factual reliability and safety.

The study suggests that the increased susceptibility to adversarial attacks seen in warmth fine-tuned models may stem from data construction rather than an inherent trade-off with empathetic adaptation. By adjusting the training data to reflect low agreeableness in user turns, the researchers achieved safer empathetic fine-tuning without relying on safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objectives. Representational analysis indicates this method reduces the alignment between warmth and compliance in the models' latent space, contributing to improved safety.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for social warmth degrades factual reliability and increases sycophancy. We investigate a related but distinct failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety, making models more susceptible to jailbreaks and harmful output generation. We examine whether this reflects an inherent consequence of empathetic adaptation or an artifact of data construction. To address this, we introduce a persona-driven rewriting pipeline that conditions user turns on low agreeableness and pairs this with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. Across three experiments on four models, our approach reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates relative to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines, while preserving conversational warmth. Representational probing provides suggestive evidence that this conditioning reduces the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space. These results show that safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone, without safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objective.

items.title: Researchers introduce The Simulacrum, a neural network framework using decision-theoretic pretraining for near-optimal time-series forecasting and inference with zero-shot capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Simulacrum: Decision-Theoretic Pretraining for Near-Optimal Time-Series Forecasting and Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have developed The Simulacrum, a neural network framework that uses decision-theoretic pretraining to create near-optimal estimators for time-series forecasting and inference. By training on simulations from a specified generative model and decision objective, the framework produces neural estimators capable of zero-shot inference on new time series, offering forecasts, parameter estimates, predictive intervals, and model selection. This approach directly targets finite-sample properties such as risk minimization, bias control, and calibration, enabling performance that surpasses traditional methods like maximum likelihood estimation and AICc-based model selection within the same model classes.

The framework demonstrates competitive or state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world forecasting benchmarks, even when trained solely on simulated structural models. It addresses challenges such as finite-sample bias and miscalibration in autoregressive models and the forecast combination puzzle, highlighting its ability to solve analytically complex or computationally intensive time series problems. By allowing explicit control over decision-theoretic trade-offs, The Simulacrum offers analysts efficient, tailored estimation tools suited to their specific analytical goals.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a neural network-based framework for learning time series estimators through a process we term decision-theoretic pretraining. Analysts specify a generative world, a distribution over data-generating processes, and a target decision objective. A neural network trained on stratified simulations from this world approximates the corresponding optimal decision rule, yielding a neural estimator that provides forecasts, parameter estimates, predictive intervals, or model-selection for zero-shot inference on previously unseen time series. The joint specification of the generative world and objective enables the estimators to directly approximate process-level, finite-sample properties: near-optimal risk, bias control, minimax performance, and uniform calibration. Our experiments demonstrate that these neural estimators can outperform traditional baselines such as maximum likelihood estimation and model selection via AICc, for the same model structural model classes. Furthermore, even when trained purely on simulations of structural models, they achieve competitive or state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on major real-world benchmarks, compared with statistical, neural or large pre-trained models. We illustrate the framework by addressing two longstanding challenges: finite-sample bias and miscalibration in AR(p) models, and the forecast combination puzzle. These applications highlight the approach's main advantage: its ability to approximate solutions to analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive time series problems, including complex structural equations or optimality criteria. Ultimately, by enabling explicit control over decision-theoretic trade-offs, the framework equips analysts with highly efficient estimation tools tailored to their specific analytical needs.

items.title: Researchers introduce Bifocal Diffusion Language Models with asymmetric bidirectional context, achieving up to 12.9× throughput over bidirectional dLLMs and 2.9× speedup over autoregressive baselines in batch serving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Bifocal Diffusion Language Models: Asymmetric Bidirectional Context for Parallel Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Bifocal Diffusion Language Models (dLLMs) that address a key challenge in language model design by combining asymmetric bidirectional context. Their approach, called R2LM (Right-to-Left Mamba), integrates standard causal attention for left-context with a lightweight reverse mechanism to provide compressed right-side context, enabling efficient parallel decoding with KV caching. This design achieves up to 12.9 times higher throughput than traditional bidirectional dLLMs and up to 2.9 times speedup over autoregressive baselines in batch serving, while maintaining or exceeding generation quality benchmarks.

The team demonstrated these results through extensive experiments involving continued pretraining of the Qwen3-1.7B model on 60 billion tokens. R2LM effectively balances the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency by preserving cache compatibility and incorporating right-side context without performance loss. This innovation offers a promising direction for improving the speed and quality of language model inference in practical applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) recover masked tokens in parallel, offering significant speedups over autoregressive (AR) generation. However, such promising frameworks face a fundamental architectural design dilemma: \ding{182} Adopting bidirectional attention achieves strong generation quality by allowing each position to access the full context, but is inherently incompatible with KV caching, limiting inference throughput in batch-serving scenarios; \ding{183} Conversely, causal attention enables efficient cached inference but loses all right-side context, substantially degrading generation quality. This paper introduces Bifocal dLLMs, a new paradigm that resolves this dilemma through \emph{asymmetric bidirectional context}. Analogous to bifocal lenses, we instantiate the paradigm as \textbf{R2LM} (Right-to-Left Mamba), which combines two complementary mechanisms: $a$) standard causal attention providing precise left-context with full KV cache compatibility, while $b$) a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar supplying compressed right-side context without breaking cacheability. Comprehensive experiments on continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B with 60B tokens demonstrate that R2LM achieves $2.4\times$ to $12.9\times$ higher throughput than bidirectional dLLMs and $1.9\times$ to $2.9\times$ speedup over AR baselines in batch serving through parallel decoding with KV caching, while exceeding the causal baseline on most benchmarks and surpassing the bidirectional dLLM on average.

items.title: Researchers present KG2Cypher, a data-centric pipeline for building enterprise text-to-Cypher systems with LoRA-based inference, achieving over 95% exact match and 99.9% execution rate in Korean enterprise tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KG2Cypher: Data-Centric Pipeline for Building Enterprise Text-to-Cypher Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed KG2Cypher, a data-centric pipeline designed to create enterprise text-to-Cypher systems from existing knowledge graphs (KGs). This approach generates executable Cypher queries from graph facts and uses large language models (LLMs) to produce corresponding natural-language questions. The system then validates these pairs through LLM judgment and human review, converting them into candidate-aware supervised fine-tuning data. The pipeline was tested in Korean enterprise environments, where short search queries and schema variations pose challenges for language grounding. items.title: Researchers propose Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework for resource-adaptive LLM inference that dynamically adjusts computation based on input and runtime resource budgets, achieving up to 34% layer sparsity with minimal accuracy loss on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: End-to-End Dynamic Sparsity for Resource-Adaptive LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework designed for resource-adaptive inference in large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional static models that use a fixed computational graph, L2A dynamically adjusts computation based on both the input and the available runtime resource budget. This approach integrates lightweight gating networks into LLMs to optimize task performance, logical consistency, and resource usage by selectively skipping layers, pruning heads, and reducing reasoning tokens according to real-time resource constraints.

L2A was tested on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B models, achieving up to 34% layer sparsity while maintaining accuracy within 0.6% of dense baselines on benchmark tasks like GSM8K. This adaptive method outperforms static or heuristic baselines, which require separate tuning and suffer larger accuracy drops under similar inference times. By tracing the compute-accuracy trade-off frontier, L2A enables LLMs to maximize reasoning depth when resources allow and enforce efficiency when budgets tighten, making it well-suited for dynamic cloud environments with fluctuating resource availability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inference is typically deployed under a static resource assumption, where models execute a fixed computational graph regardless of the runtime environment. However, real-world cloud infrastructure is inherently dynamic, characterized by fluctuating availability (e.g., spot instance preemption) and tiered Quality-of-Service requirements. In such volatile settings, static models are inflexible: they either crash under resource constraints or waste compute on redundant operations. To bridge this gap, we propose Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework for resource-adaptive inference. Unlike prior methods that condition only on input difficulty, we formulate inference as a constrained allocation problem conditioned on both the input and the runtime resource budget itself. We introduce lightweight, budget-conditioned and input-aware gating networks integrated into the LLM. These gates are trained via a unified objective that jointly optimizes task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs along three axes matching how real-world dynamics manifest: layer skipping for memory and depth pressure, head pruning for throughput contention, and reasoning-token reduction for latency tightening. This lets the model learn a budget-aware policy beyond input difficulty alone: it adaptively configures its computational footprint with respect to real-time resource dynamics, maximizing reasoning depth when resources permit while enforcing strict frugality when budgets tighten. A single L2A model traces the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B: at up to 34% realized layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same gap holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks, while every static or heuristic baseline requires a separately tuned model and still drops by 5-10% at comparable inference time.

items.title: Researchers propose Flexformer, a flexible linear Transformer with learnable attention kernels using trainable spectral frequencies, achieving improved efficiency and performance on long-sequence tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Flexformer: Flexible Linear Transformer with Learnable Attention Kernel
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Flexformer, a flexible linear Transformer model that improves efficiency and performance on long-sequence tasks by learning attention kernels through trainable spectral frequencies. Unlike traditional Transformer models that face quadratic complexity and kernel-based linear attention methods that use fixed or weakly learnable kernels, Flexformer employs a fully data-driven approach to learn a wide range of attention kernels, including both stationary and more expressive nonstationary variants.

Built on random Fourier feature-based linear attention, Flexformer demonstrates superior results in language modeling and sequence classification compared to baseline models. It can also be distilled from pretrained Transformers to replicate softmax attention and shows strong kernel transferability across different domains, making it a promising solution for scalable and effective long-sequence processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer models rely on attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies but suffer from quadratic complexity, limiting their scalability to long sequences. Kernel-based linear attention reduces this complexity but typically relies on fixed or weakly learnable kernels, restricting expressiveness and performance. In this work, we propose Flexformer, a flexible linear Transformer that learns attention kernels in a fully data-driven manner. Flexformer builds on random Fourier feature-based linear attention and treats spectral frequencies as trainable parameters, enabling the model to learn a broad family of attention kernels. We develop both stationary and nonstationary variants, with the latter offering strictly greater expressiveness. Extensive experiments on language modeling and sequence classification demonstrate that Flexformer consistently outperforms baselines. Moreover, Flexformer can be effectively distilled from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax attention and exhibits strong kernel transferability across domains, achieving both high efficiency and competitive performance on long-sequence tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose RS-Diffuser, a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework using distributional value critics to improve safety and robustness in reinforcement learning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RS-Diffuser: Risk-Sensitive Diffusion Planning with Distributional Value Guidance
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RS-Diffuser, a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework designed to enhance safety and robustness in reinforcement learning tasks. This approach integrates diffusion-based trajectory generation with distributional value critics to better account for rare but catastrophic outcomes, which are often overlooked by traditional risk-neutral diffusion planners. RS-Diffuser enables flexible behavior adjustment—risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking—by modifying a risk parameter during inference without retraining the model.

The framework includes a diffusion planner for future state trajectories, an inverse dynamics model for decoding actions, and a Monte Carlo distributional critic that estimates the full return distribution using quantile regression. During sampling, it applies risk-sensitive guidance based on tail-aware objectives like Conditional Value at Risk to steer trajectory generation toward desired risk profiles. Extensive testing on risk-sensitive benchmarks, including D4RL and robot navigation tasks, demonstrated that RS-Diffuser achieves state-of-the-art performance by improving overall returns and worst-case robustness while reducing safety violations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning enables policy learning from fixed datasets without additional environment interaction, making it appealing for safety-critical applications where online exploration is costly or unsafe. Diffusion-based decision-making methods have recently achieved strong performance in offline RL by modeling rich, multimodal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion planners are typically risk-neutral and therefore may overlook rare but catastrophic outcomes that are crucial in real-world deployment. In this work, we propose RS-Diffuser, a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework that combines diffusion-based trajectory generation with distributional value critics. RS-Diffuser learns a diffusion planner over future state trajectories, a separate inverse dynamics model for action decoding, and a Monte Carlo distributional critic that estimates the full return distribution of candidate plans through quantile regression. At sampling time, we incorporate a risk-sensitive guidance signal into the denoising process, using gradients computed from tail-aware objectives such as Conditional Value at Risk to steer generation toward desired risk profiles. As a result, a single trained model can flexibly produce risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking behaviors by changing only the inference-time risk parameter. Extensive experiments on risk-sensitive D4RL and risky robot navigation benchmarks demonstrate that RS-Diffuser achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving both overall return and worst-case robustness while reducing safety violations.

items.title: Researchers propose Activation Amplification and Attenuation (A3), a lightweight module that improves neural network adversarial robustness by dynamically rescaling activations with minimal overhead [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Adversarial Robustness via Activation Amplification and Attenuation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Activation Amplification and Attenuation (A3), a lightweight module designed to enhance the adversarial robustness of neural networks by dynamically rescaling activations. A3 uses a learnable mask and scaling factor based on original activation magnitudes to amplify or attenuate signals, helping to mitigate the impact of adversarial perturbations with minimal changes to the network.

The module operates by flipping the sign of the scaling operation to switch between amplification and attenuation modes, using amplified signals as negative references for new contrastive and ranking loss functions. Experiments show that training in amplification mode improves robustness in attenuation mode, and A3 achieves these benefits with few additional parameters and negligible computational overhead. The approach has been validated across various backbones, datasets, and training methods, consistently improving adversarial defense. The code is publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The existence of adversarial attacks is often attributed to the presence of non-robust features in neural networks. While prior defenses reduce their impact via pruning, masking, or feature recalibration, we instead propose to jointly learn to amplify and attenuate these signals through a simple activation scaling mechanism. To this end, we introduce Activation Amplification and Attenuation (A3), a lightweight plug-in module that enhances adversarial robustness with minimal modifications of the activations. A3 dynamically rescales the activations using a learnable mask and a scaling factor derived from the original activation magnitudes. The influence of adversarial perturbations can be amplified or attenuated using the same learnable parameters by simply flipping the sign of the scaling operation. The amplified signals serve as negative references to construct novel contrastive and ranking loss functions. Experimental analysis shows that learning to degrade the predictions in amplification mode simultaneously improves adversarial robustness in attenuation mode. Moreover, A3 relies on only a small number of learnable parameters, with most of its behavior being determined by the scaling mechanism rather than additional network capacity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating A3 into different backbones, datasets, and training methods consistently improves adversarial robustness while introducing negligible computational and memory overhead compared to existing plug-in modules. Code is available at: https://github.com/tgoncalv/A3.

items.title: Study finds output-space allocation cost alignment improves accuracy but increases perplexity in calibration-guided compression of Qwen3-8B and shows minor effects on Llama-3.2-1B at lower compression ratios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Output-Space Allocation Costs for Calibration-Guided LLM Compression: An Empirical Study
items.summary:
A recent study examines the impact of aligning allocation costs with output-space objectives in calibration-guided compression of large language models (LLMs). Using the ROCKET method on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, the researchers found that output-space cost alignment improved average accuracy by 0.8 percentage points across eight zero-shot benchmarks but increased perplexity on WikiText by 16%, indicating a tradeoff between accuracy and perplexity. The study also observed a strong correlation between weight-space and output-space errors, which limited the divergence in allocation and resulted in modest overall effects.

When applied to Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, the difference between using weight-space and output-space allocation costs was minimal, with nearly identical accuracy and perplexity results. This suggests that the choice of allocation cost function has a minor effect at lower compression ratios. The findings highlight that different allocation objectives may favor different downstream performance metrics, providing insights for optimizing training-free compression methods for LLMs.
items.description:
A recent study examines the impact of aligning allocation costs with output-space objectives in calibration-guided compression of large language models (LLMs). Using the ROCKET method on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, the researchers found that output-space cost alignment improved average accuracy by 0.8 percentage points across eight zero-shot benchmarks but increased perplexity on WikiText by 16%, indicating a tradeoff between accuracy and perplexity. The study also observed a strong correlation between weight-space and output-space errors, which limited the divergence in allocation and resulted in modest overall effects.

When applied to Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, the difference between using weight-space and output-space allocation costs was minimal, with nearly identical accuracy and perplexity results. This suggests that the choice of allocation cost function has a minor effect at lower compression ratios. The findings highlight that different allocation objectives may favor different downstream performance metrics, providing insights for optimizing training-free compression methods for LLMs.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training-free compression methods for large language models (LLMs) often use calibration data to guide compression decisions. ROCKET, a recent method combining sparse-dictionary factorization with multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) allocation, derives its per-layer factorization from an output reconstruction objective but uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP allocation cost. We investigate whether aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective improves compressed model fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50\% compression, our ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy across 8 zero-shot benchmarks (53.1\% vs 52.3\%), but increases WikiText perplexity by 16\% (61.46 vs 52.98). This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff reveals that different allocation objectives favor different downstream metrics. The high correlation ($>$0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20\% compression, the two methods produce near-identical results (53.3\% vs 53.5\% accuracy, 14.45 vs 14.66 PPL), suggesting that the effect of the cost function is minor at lower compression ratios.

items.title: Researchers introduce SHIFT, a gate-modulated activation steering framework to mitigate knowledge conflicts in retrieval-augmented generation by adaptively regulating LLM internal activations with under 0.01% trainable parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SHIFT: Gate-Modulated Activation Steering for Knowledge Conflict Mitigation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SHIFT, a new framework designed to address knowledge conflicts in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems by adaptively regulating internal activations of large language models (LLMs). SHIFT introduces a lightweight gate module that modulates neuron-level activations with fewer than 0.01% trainable parameters, allowing the backbone model to remain frozen while resolving conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge during response generation.

Unlike previous neuron-editing approaches that risk unintended effects on broader model functions, SHIFT's gate modulation enables LLMs to dynamically balance contextual and stored knowledge. Extensive testing across six datasets demonstrates SHIFT's effectiveness compared to existing methods, with all related datasets and code made publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by incorporating external knowledge to support response generation. However, conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge have emerged as a critical challenge in RAG systems. To mitigate such conflicts, numerous studies have attempted to identify and edit knowledge-related internal neurons, aiming to improve the ability of LLMs to rely on contextual evidence during generation. However, these neuron-level approaches may introduce unintended cascading effects that compromise the general capabilities of LLMs, as the modified neurons are often entangled with broader model behaviors and functionalities. In this paper, we introduce SHIFT, a novel framework that reformulates neuron-level modification as learnable gate modulation, allowing LLMs to adaptively regulate internal activations for knowledge conflict resolution. Technically, our SHIFT equips LLMs with a lightweight gate module and optimizes fewer than 0.01% trainable parameters while keeping the backbone model frozen. During generation, the gate module adjusts the model's internal representations to adaptively leverage contextual and parametric knowledge. Extensive experiments on six datasets validate the effectiveness of our SHIFT in comparison with various competing baselines. All datasets and code are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/SHIFT.

items.title: Researchers propose NLL-guided training-free method to select full-attention layers for sliding-window adaptation, achieving 64.6% accuracy with 25% full-attention layers on LongMemEval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: NLL-Guided Full-Attention Layer Selection for Training-Free Sliding-Window Adaptation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a training-free method called NLL-guided layer selection to optimize hybrid attention models that combine full and sliding-window attention for efficient long-context inference. This approach identifies which layers should retain full attention by measuring the negative log-likelihood degradation when switching layers from full to sliding-window attention. Tested on LongMemEval with the Qwen3-4B model, the method achieved 64.6% accuracy using only 25% of layers with full attention, matching the performance of a baseline using 50% full-attention layers while reducing computational costs by half.

The NLL-guided selection outperformed existing periodic and LightTransfer-style baselines by significant margins, demonstrating that its effectiveness stems from addressing long-range attention needs rather than general layer sensitivity. The method requires only about 15 minutes of one-time calibration, offering a practical advancement in balancing efficiency and accuracy for deploying large language models with long-context capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid attention models that mix full and sliding-window attention across layers offer a promising approach to efficient long-context inference, but the critical question of \emph{which layers} should retain full attention remains unsolved. Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns or attention-based heuristics that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. We propose NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method that directly measures each layer's importance by computing the negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention. On LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, our method achieves 64.6\% accuracy using only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0\%) while halving the computational budget. NLL-guided selection outperforms the SWAA-reported periodic 1/4-FA baseline by 10.4 percentage points and a matched LightTransfer-style baseline by 26.4 percentage points. De-confounding analysis shows the signal is consistent with long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity. The method requires only $\sim$15 minutes of one-time calibration, advancing the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment.

items.title: Researchers find position bias correction insufficient to match iterative attention sorting in long-context language models, with single-pass debiasing closing only part of the accuracy gap [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Position Bias Correction is Insufficient for One-Pass Attention Sorting
items.summary: Researchers have investigated the effectiveness of position bias correction in long-context language models, which tend to underutilize information in middle positions. They proposed Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting, a method that estimates and corrects position bias to enable single-pass document sorting. However, experiments on two models showed that this approach either matched uncorrected single-pass sorting or only partially closed the accuracy gap compared to iterative Attention Sorting, which reorders documents multiple times based on attention patterns.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context language models suffer from position bias, where information in middle positions is underutilized. Attention Sorting addresses this by iteratively reordering documents based on attention patterns, but its multiple sort-and-generate cycles increase deployment cost. We hypothesize that position bias is the primary bottleneck and propose Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting, which estimates a per-prompt position-bias curve from the low-attention majority of documents and uses it to correct raw attention scores (via subtraction or division) to enable single-pass sorting. Our experiments on two models refute this hypothesis in the tested setting: on LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct, debiasing produces identical results to uncalibrated single-pass sorting (94.83\% containment accuracy), while on YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k, debiasing improves accuracy by 8.67 percentage points but remains 14.84pp behind iterative sorting, closing only 37\% of the gap. These results suggest that position-bias correction is insufficient to match iterative sorting, and that repeated reordering provides additional benefits beyond bias correction.

items.title: Researchers present HPC-aware method for knowledge distillation that decouples teacher-student partitioning, achieving up to 67% higher samples-per-second than TRL on production HPC clusters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimizing Teacher-Student Partitioning for Scalable Knowledge Distillation on HPC Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a high-performance computing (HPC)-aware method for knowledge distillation that decouples the partitioning of teacher and student models. This approach leverages the asymmetry between the larger teacher and smaller student models in terms of memory and communication needs, achieving up to 67% higher samples-per-second compared to the widely used TRL library on production HPC clusters.

The method combines vertical and horizontal model partitioning and uses an analytical expression to identify optimal splitting strategies, avoiding unnecessary data structures for the teacher model. By exploiting topology-aware parallelism and the distinct characteristics of teacher and student models, this technique significantly accelerates knowledge distillation training in large-scale HPC environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) enables training smaller student models under the guidance of larger teacher models, and the widely adopted TRL library implements it. Yet, TRL treats both models symmetrically, missing opportunities to exploit their pronounced asymmetry in memory footprint, and communication requirements. This paper presents an HPC-aware methodology for KD that decouples teacher and student partitioning efficiently. Our approach achieves up to 67% higher samples-per-second than TRL by avoiding unnecessary teacher-model data structures and selecting the best split strategy. We combine vertical and horizontal partitioning of models, deriving an analytical expression that identifies the existence of inflection points between splitting regimes. These results showed that exploiting teacher--student asymmetry through topology-aware parallelism notably accelerated GKD training on production HPC clusters at our company

items.title: Researchers develop parameter-efficient quantum-inspired fast weight programmers for multi-step traffic-matrix forecasting, outperforming LSTM models with reduced resource use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Parameter-Efficient Quantum-Inspired Fast Weight Programmers for Traffic-Matrix Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed parameter-efficient quantum-inspired fast weight programmers to improve multi-step traffic-matrix forecasting, a critical task in network traffic engineering. These models, based on gated quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network fast-weight programmers (QKAN-FWPs), predict future network demand more accurately and with fewer resources compared to traditional long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. The best-performing variant, G-QKANFWP, achieved the lowest root-mean-square error while using only about 22% of the resources of a larger LSTM model.

The study evaluated three QKAN variants against matched-size and larger LSTM models under a fixed training budget, demonstrating that the quantum-inspired models outperform both classical LSTMs and gated fast-weight programmers. Analysis of convergence and channel-wise performance further confirmed the efficiency and accuracy advantages of the quantum-inspired approach. These findings suggest that combining classical slow programmers with quantum-inspired fast programmers offers a promising design for resource-conscious network traffic forecasting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traffic matrices (TMs) capture network-wide origin-destination demand and are central to traffic engineering, yet accurate whole-matrix forecasting remains challenging when prediction must be performed under the memory, update, and training-budget constraints of online network control. This paper investigates whether compact quantum-inspired recurrent models can provide effective TM forecasts without relying on dedicated graph, transformer, or diffusion modules. We adapt gated quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network fast-weight programmers (QKAN-FWPs) to direct multi-step Abilene TM forecasting, where each model predicts the next 20 five-minute frames of a 144-channel origin-destination (OD) matrix from a two-hour history. We benchmark three QKAN placement variants against a matched-size long short-term memory (LSTM) network, a larger LSTM, and a classical gated fast-weight programmer under a shared fixed-budget training protocol. Among the evaluated recurrent models, G-QKANFWP achieves the best pooled root-mean-square error (RMSE), while using only 22.4% of the larger LSTM. It also outperforms both the matched-size LSTM and the classical G-FWP baseline, indicating that the gain is not due to gated fast-weight framework alone. Convergence and channel-wise analyses further show that the quantum-inspired variants obtain lower validation-loss area under the learning curve (AULC) than matched-size recurrent baselines, while G-QKANFWP and GQKAN-FWP achieve substantially more OD-channel wins. These results identify a classical slow programmer with a quantum-inspired fast programmer as a promising accuracy-efficiency design for resource-conscious network traffic-matrix forecasting.

items.title: Researchers present Pepti-drift, a toxicity-aware framework generating antigen-specific peptides by attracting binding features and repelling toxicity in peptide embedding space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pepti-drift: Toxicity-Repulsive Drifting for Antigen-Conditioned Discrete Peptide Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Pepti-drift, a novel framework designed to generate antigen-specific peptides while minimizing toxicity. This approach uses a toxicity-aware latent refinement process that guides peptide candidates toward binding features specific to an antigen and away from regions associated with toxicity within a peptide embedding space. The method addresses the challenge that binding-promoting and toxicity-associated features often overlap in peptide representations.

Pepti-drift employs a warm-up strategy to balance these competing objectives by initially focusing on attracting peptides with binding properties and subsequently increasing repulsion from toxic regions. This single antigen-conditioned drift step offers a promising advancement for therapeutic peptide discovery by improving specificity and safety in peptide design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Peptides are a promising therapeutic modality that combine the chemical tunability of small molecules with the target specificity of macromolecular therapeutics. However, designing antigen-specific binding peptides while avoiding toxicity remains a major challenge for therapeutic peptide discovery. Here, we present Pepti-drift, a toxicity-aware latent refinement framework that generates peptide candidates through a single antigen-conditioned drift step. In a peptide embedding space, Pepti-drift learns to attract generated peptide latents toward antigen-matched binding peptides while repelling them from toxicity-associated regions. This is challenging because binding-promoting physicochemical features often overlap with toxicity-associated features in peptide representation space. To address this, we introduce a warm-up strategy to stabilize this competing objective by first learning binding-oriented attraction and then increasing toxicity repulsion.
