items.originalTitle: WattLayer: Get Layers Right to Estimate Inference Energy of Neural Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed WattLayer, a task-independent, layer-wise model designed to estimate the energy consumption of neural network inference with a median error of 19.6%. The model was tested on over 100,000 layers from 295 neural network architectures across three common AI tasks and three different hardware platforms, outperforming existing methods. WattLayer's layer-wise approach allows it to generalize to new tasks without requiring full retraining by leveraging shared layers across architectures.

This methodology provides a standardized and precise tool for estimating AI inference energy consumption, addressing growing concerns about the environmental impact of AI. By enabling more accurate energy assessments, WattLayer offers valuable insights and practical support for designing energy-efficient AI systems across diverse applications and hardware configurations.

items.title: Researchers investigate activation-based memorization indicators to detect overfitting early during low-sample recalibration of sEMG deep learning decoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Applicability of memorization indicators for early spotting of overfitting while recalibrating sEMG-decoders on low sample sizes
items.summary:
Researchers have explored the use of activation-based memorization indicators to detect overfitting early during the low-sample recalibration of deep learning models for surface electromyography (sEMG). Since collecting large datasets for subject-specific calibration is challenging, traditional overfitting detection methods are often impractical. The study demonstrates that monitoring activation statistics of neural network units during fine-tuning can reveal early signs of performance degradation without requiring additional validation data.

The team conducted transfer learning experiments using a convolutional neural network pre-trained on multiple subjects and fine-tuned on individual users with limited repetitions. They observed that decreases in test accuracy corresponded with characteristic changes in activation rates of the network's last hidden layer. These findings suggest that activation-based memorization indicators offer a promising approach for identifying unsuccessful learning in low-sample sEMG calibration scenarios, potentially improving the reliability of personalized deep learning decoders.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models for surface electromyography (sEMG) can benefit substantially from subject-specific (re-)calibration, since no sufficiently large and diverse datasets are available to train fully generic decoders. However, for user acceptance, the number of repetitions that can realistically be collected during calibration is severely limited, which increases the risk of overfitting and, in extreme cases, can even degrade performance compared to the uncalibrated model. Classical overfitting indicators such as validation performance and regularization with early stopping are difficult to apply in this low-sample regime, as they require additional held-out data that is rarely available in practical calibration scenarios. In this work, we investigate a recently proposed class of memorization indicators based solely on the activation statistics of rectified linear units (ReLU) in deep neural networks, which can be computed directly from training data without any extra validation set. We conduct a transferlearning experiment on a benchmark sEMG dataset, where a convolutional neural network is first pre-trained on multiple subjects and subsequently fine-tuned on individual users using only a small number of repetitions. During calibration, we monitor both decoding performance and the activation behaviour of the last hidden layer. Our results provide first evidence that decreases in test accuracy during fine-tuning are ac companied by characteristic changes in activation rates, indicating that activation-based memorization indicators are a promising tool for early spotting of unsuccessful learning in low-sample sEMG calibration settings.

items.title: Researchers propose GNBAN, a graph neural basis attention network for scalable, interpretable long-horizon demand forecasting across large retail entity sets, improving accuracy by 4-5% on major benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GNBAN: Graph Neural Basis Attention Networks for Long-Horizon Forecasting over Large Entity Sets
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GNBAN (Graph Neural Basis Attention Network), a novel architecture designed for scalable and interpretable long-horizon demand forecasting across extensive retail hierarchies. By representing retail data as a heterogeneous graph and decomposing forecasts into trend, seasonal, and generic components, GNBAN improves accuracy by 4-5% on major benchmarks like M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales compared to existing graph-based models. Its per-basis attention mechanism allows different basis functions to specialize in distinct temporal patterns while maintaining interpretability.

GNBAN addresses challenges faced by traditional statistical and deep learning methods, which struggle with scalability and interpretability when forecasting thousands of correlated time series. The model's design enables a single system to serve an entire product catalog by leveraging relational data structures and an interpretable basis-decomposition head. Qualitative analysis confirms that the model effectively exposes underlying demand drivers without requiring additional explanation methods.

These findings demonstrate that combining scalable relational forecasting with interpretable decomposition is feasible within a unified graph-based framework, offering promising advancements for demand forecasting in large retail settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Demand forecasting at the bottom of a retail hierarchy requires predicting tens of thousands of correlated long-horizon series across products, stores, and regions. Modern systems must scale across massive catalogs, capture shared demand dynamics, and remain interpretable enough to be trusted. Classical statistical methods need a separate model per series and are hard to manage at scale; deep autoregressive models struggle as the joint state grows to tens of thousands of dimensions; and recent graph-based forecasters, while capturing cross-entity dependencies, often produce opaque long-horizon forecasts. We propose GNBAN (Graph Neural Basis Attention Network), an end-to-end architecture combining heterogeneous graph representation learning with an interpretable basis-decomposition head. Retail data are represented directly as a heterogeneous graph derived from the relational schema, so a single model serves the entire catalog. Rather than predicting the horizon directly, GNBAN decomposes each forecast into trend, seasonal, and generic components. Its key innovation is a per-basis attention mechanism: each basis function keeps its own learnable query and retrieves information independently from the entity's historical neighborhood, letting different bases specialize to distinct temporal patterns while preserving interpretability. On two large-scale benchmarks, M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales, evaluated under matched protocols, GNBAN improves volume-weighted WRMSSE by roughly 4-5% over a matched graph baseline. Qualitative analysis shows the learned decomposition exposes trend, seasonal, and residual demand drivers without post-hoc explanation methods. These results demonstrate that scalable relational forecasting and interpretable forecast decomposition can be achieved together in a unified graph-based framework.

items.title: Researchers study temporal fusion strategies for named entity recognition in historical French and German texts, finding late fusion methods improve robustness and temporal generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Study of Temporal Fusion Strategies for Named Entity Recognition in Historical Texts
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated how to improve named entity recognition (NER) in historical French and German texts by incorporating temporal metadata into language models. They explored various lightweight fusion strategies, including early and late fusion methods, to embed both absolute and relative temporal information into Transformer-based architectures. Their study found that late fusion techniques, such as cross-attention and adapters, enhance the robustness and temporal generalization of NER models, especially in earlier and noisier historical periods.

The research addresses the challenge of temporal variation in historical texts, where entity forms and prominence change over time, complicating NER tasks. By systematically comparing fusion strategies on historical datasets, the study demonstrates that integrating temporal context at later stages of the model yields better performance than early fusion approaches. This work contributes to advancing natural language processing methods for diachronic text analysis and improving the handling of temporal dynamics in historical document processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal variation poses a unique challenge for named entity recognition (NER) in historical texts, where entities drift in surface form and salience across time. While language models (LMs) have made progress in various NLP tasks, their ability to reason about temporality, especially in diachronic contexts, remains limited or at least, questionable. In this paper, we systematically study how temporal metadata can be structurally embedded into NER models using a range of lightweight fusion strategies. We experiment with both absolute and relative temporal representations, injected into Transformer-based architectures via early or late fusion mechanisms such as cross-attention, adapters, and concatenation. Our evaluations on French and German historical datasets reveal that late fusion strategies yield more robust and temporally generalisable performance, particularly in early and noisy periods.

items.title: Researchers extend Werewolf game with a Jester role to test multi-hop theory of mind in LLMs, finding Jester wins 60-70% of games across GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Triadic Werewolf: A Jester Role for Multi-Hop Theory of Mind in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have enhanced the classic Werewolf social deduction game by introducing a Jester role, creating a triadic incentive structure to better evaluate multi-hop theory of mind in large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional dyadic games where cues point to a single hidden side, the Jester wins by being voted out, requiring models to reason across three opposing utility functions. Testing this setup on GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B showed the Jester winning 60-70% of games, while Werewolves rarely exceeded 20%, highlighting complex multi-agent reasoning challenges for LLMs.

The study found that GPT-4.1 often made self-defeating moves by voting out the Jester early, whereas DeepSeek demonstrated a nuanced strategy of appearing suspicious without intentional suspicion, benefiting most from self-learning. These results suggest that triadic games reveal layers of strategic reasoning that simpler dyadic games fail to expose, offering a more rigorous test of theory-of-mind capabilities in language models.

items.title: Researchers propose two-stage fine-tuning with reinforcement learning to generate protein sequences matching targeted amino-acid compositions while preserving sequence quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Two-Stage Fine-Tuning for Protein Sequence Generation with Targeted Amino-Acid Composition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a two-stage fine-tuning approach combining domain-adaptive fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to generate protein sequences that match specific amino-acid composition targets while maintaining sequence quality and diversity. This method addresses the challenge of steering protein language models toward explicit distributional design goals, particularly relevant for synthetic feed protein design where amino-acid composition affects nutritional value.

The proposed pipeline first fine-tunes a protein language model on an in-domain dataset, then applies iterative reward-weighted fine-tuning via reinforcement learning anchored to the initial model. Evaluations on two amino-acid compositions show that fine-tuning alone brings sequences close to the target composition, while reinforcement learning enforces additional sequence constraints. The study also compares different reward designs and training stages, confirming that the approach achieves composition alignment without compromising sequence plausibility.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein language models are standard priors for biological sequence generation, but steering them toward explicit distributional design targets remains largely unexplored. We study a constrained protein generation problem in which sequences must match a desired amino-acid (AA) composition profile while preserving plausible sequence statistics and diversity. The motivating application is synthetic feed protein design, where the AA composition of dietary proteins directly determines their nutritional value. We propose a two-stage pipeline in which domain-adaptive fine-tuning (FT) on an in-domain protein dataset is followed by iterative reward-weighted FT via reinforcement learning (RL) anchored against the FT model as a frozen reference. We evaluate the pipeline on two AA compositions and find that FT brings the average composition close to the target, while the subsequent RL enforces specific sequence constraints that FT alone cannot satisfy. We additionally evaluate the design choices of the proposed composition reward term against two baselines and an ablated variant, isolate the contribution of each training stage, and verify that AA composition alignment is achieved without degrading sequence quality.

items.title: Researchers propose a multi-stage explainable framework using LLaMA-3.1 and SHAP to interpret speech-based cognitive impairment detection models with 72.11% F1 on NIA PREPARE benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Black-Box to Clinical Insight: A Multi-Stage Explainable Framework for Speech-Based Cognitive Impairment Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-stage explainability framework that enhances the interpretability of transformer-based models used for speech-based cognitive impairment detection. This framework integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for token attribution, theory-informed linguistic features, and a four-stage reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct. It builds on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network model, achieving an F1 score of 72.11% on the NIA PREPARE benchmark, and translates model outputs into four cognitive-linguistic dimensions such as lexical richness and semantic coherence.

Physician evaluations on 70 stratified English samples showed strong alignment between the framework's explanations and patient cognitive profiles. Additionally, the framework received a System Usability Scale score of 82 out of 100, indicating its potential for integration into clinical workflows to provide noninvasive and accessible cognitive impairment screening.

items.title: Researchers introduce a synthetic multimodal NLP pipeline combining dialogue transcripts, audio analysis, and rule-based scoring to detect insurance fraud at first notice of loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dialogue to Detection: A Multimodal Hybrid NLP Pipeline for Insurance Fraud Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a synthetic multimodal natural language processing pipeline designed to detect insurance fraud at the first notice of loss (FNOL). This approach integrates agent-customer dialogue transcripts, audio analysis, and rule-based scoring to identify indicators such as narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and repeated voices across cases. The system combines automatic speech recognition, speaker diarisation, named entity recognition, regex-based feature extraction, and large language model retrieval to generate a risk score that balances sensitivity with false positives.

The framework replicates FNOL conditions by generating two-speaker audio and dialogue data, enabling comprehensive evaluation beyond text-only methods. Validation of the dataset and individual components demonstrates the pipeline's stability and potential for transfer to real-world applications, providing a reproducible baseline for multimodal insurance fraud detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Insurance fraud imposes substantial financial losses and operational inefficiencies, raising premiums and impacting trust among legitimate policyholders. Early detection at FNOL remains a persistent challenge. Existing approaches rely largely on private, text-only datasets, limiting progress on multimodal methods that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. We introduce a synthetic multimodal framework that replicates FNOL conditions. It generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, performs ASR and diarisation. Downstream modules combine NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings in a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while balancing sensitivity and false positives. Dataset validation and component-level evaluations show stability and transfer potential, offering a reproducible baseline beyond text-only fraud detection.

items.title: Researchers introduce MLVC, a multi-platform neural video codec achieving real-time 100 FPS performance and over 70% BD-rate improvement on VCD benchmark across Apple, Intel, and Qualcomm NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MLVC: Multi-platform Learned Video Codec for Real-World Deployment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MLVC, a multi-platform neural video codec that achieves real-time encoding and decoding at 100 frames per second on common NPUs from Apple, Intel, and Qualcomm. MLVC addresses the challenges of cross-platform incompatibility and high computational costs seen in previous neural codecs by explicitly transmitting scale parameters to ensure consistent entropy coding across devices. This approach avoids decoding failures without requiring bit-exact arithmetic, enabling robust deployment across diverse hardware.

Despite a slight increase in bitrate overhead, MLVC recovers coding efficiency through architectural enhancements such as gated memory, ReGLU activation, a long-term reference recovery mechanism, and domain-specific perceptual training. On the VCD video conferencing benchmark, it delivers over 70% BD-rate improvement compared to hardware HEVC, the strongest deployable baseline, while maintaining subjective quality comparable to DCVC-RT, which lacks cross-platform support.

MLVC is the first neural video codec to combine competitive compression performance, real-time speed, and hardware robustness across multiple consumer platforms, making it suitable for widespread practical use. The researchers plan to release the code to facilitate adoption and further development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural video codecs have surpassed classical codecs in coding efficiency but remain impractical for deployment due to cross-platform incompatibility and high computational cost. Existing quantization-based solutions fail to produce deterministic results across diverse hardware platforms, leading to catastrophic decoding failures. We introduce MLVC, a hardware-robust neural video codec designed for practical cross-platform inference. The key idea is to explicitly transmit scale parameters through the hyperprior, which guarantees entropy coding consistency across devices without requiring bit-exact arithmetic. While this increases bitrate overhead, we recover most of the coding efficiency through architectural improvements (gated memory, ReGLU activation), a long-term reference recovery mechanism, and domain-specific perceptual training. On the VCD video conferencing benchmark, MLVC achieves >70% BD-rate (MOS) improvement over hardware HEVC, the strongest deployable baseline, while reaching subjective quality competitive with DCVC-RT, which cannot operate across diverse platforms. Both the encoder and decoder run at 100 FPS on average on commodity NPUs from Apple, Intel, and Qualcomm. MLVC is the first neural video codec to combine competitive compression performance, real-time speed, and cross-platform robustness across diverse consumer devices, making it suitable for widespread deployment. Code will be released.

items.title: Researchers present DG^VoiC, a speaker clustering framework for fraud investigation using anonymized real call-centre audio, achieving up to 99% accuracy in identifying repeated speakers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DG^VoiC: Speaker Clustering for Fraud Investigation under Real Call-Centre Conditions
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DG^VoiC, a speaker clustering framework designed to aid fraud investigations by analyzing anonymized call-centre audio. This system identifies repeated speakers across calls, a method that has been underutilized in fraud detection, achieving up to 99% accuracy in linking voices under real telephony conditions. The framework integrates anonymization aligned with sensitive information, speech-focused preprocessing, and cosine similarity-based clustering to verify speaker consistency and detect repeated voices among customers.

The approach was tested on 121 recordings, with a subset of 56 samples grouped into 22 speaker clusters agreed upon by human evaluators. The best-performing configuration demonstrated high metrics including 96% Adjusted Mutual Information, 95% Adjusted Rand Index, and 100% homogeneity, indicating strong clustering performance. These results suggest that speaker clustering can provide a valuable additional signal for fraud analysts, enhancing verification processes and improving detection of fraudulent activity in call-centre workflows.

While recent fraud detection methods mainly rely on structured data, text, or images, repeated speaker identity across calls remains underused as an investigative signal. This paper presents DG^VoiC, a voice clustering framework for customer verification and cross-profile speaker linking on anonymised real call-centre audio. The approach combines sensitive information-aligned anonymisation, speech-focused preprocessing, sliding-window speaker embedding extraction, and cosine similarity based clustering to identify repeated speakers under real telephony conditions. The method was evaluated on 121 recordings, with a curated reference subset of 56 samples in 22 human-agreed speaker clusters. used for validation. The best configuration achieved 96% AMI, 95% ARI, 98% completeness, 100% homogeneity, and 99% V-measure. These results show that speaker clustering can provide a strong additional signal for fraud investigation by helping analysts verify speaker consistency and surface repeated voices across customers.

These results suggest that speaker clustering can provide a valuable additional signal for fraud analysts, enhancing verification processes and improving detection of fraudulent activity in call-centre workflows.

items.title: Researchers find large language models generate more accurate answers than self-evaluate on three of four in-context QA benchmarks, challenging assumptions in self-evaluation pipelines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate? Evaluating Task Asymmetry, Mechanistic Interpretability and Transferability for In-Context QA
items.summary:
Researchers have found that large language models (LLMs) generate more accurate answers than they do when self-evaluating on three out of four in-context question-answering benchmarks, challenging the common assumption that evaluation is easier than generation. The study tested this in a controlled setting where the model judges its own generated answer based solely on a given context passage, eliminating external knowledge influences. The exception was the multi-hop MuSiQue benchmark, where self-evaluation performed better.

Analysis revealed that during evaluation, models pay significantly less attention to the context and barely review the candidate answer compared to the generation phase. Further experiments using LoRA fine-tuning showed that this asymmetry is not due to training artifacts: fine-tuning for generation led to over-acceptance of answers, while fine-tuning for evaluation degraded generation performance. These findings question key assumptions underlying self-evaluation pipelines in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation pipelines implicitly assume that evaluation is easier than generation. We test this in a controlled in-context QA setting where a context passage is the sole information source and each model judges the answer it generated, removing the parametric-knowledge confound of open-domain comparisons. Across four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and two models, evaluation is not uniformly easier: generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation on three of four, with multi-hop MuSiQue the exception. Attention analysis reveals why: evaluation attends to context 3--5x less than generation does and barely reads the candidate answer. LoRA fine-tuning confirms the asymmetry is not a training artifact: generation fine-tuning induces over-acceptance and evaluation fine-tuning degrades generation. These findings challenge core assumptions in self-evaluation pipelines.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate Large Language Models outperform traditional methods in single-truth and multi-truth data fusion tasks on benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Single and Multi Truth Data Fusion using Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) outperform traditional unsupervised truth discovery methods in data fusion tasks, which involve determining the correct values for object attributes from conflicting sources. Their study covers both single-truth scenarios, where only one correct value exists, and multi-truth scenarios, where multiple values may be valid. The evaluation was conducted using various prompting strategies on three benchmark datasets, showing consistent superiority of LLM-based approaches over methods like DART and LTM.

The research explored domain-dependent and domain-independent prompts, including zero-shot and one-shot techniques, to assess LLM performance in tabular data fusion. The findings suggest that LLMs can effectively handle complex data integration challenges across different contexts. The authors have made their code publicly available on GitHub to support further research and application in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data fusion, also known as truth discovery, is a data integration problem that aims to determine the correct value or set of values for each attribute of an object when presented with potentially conflicting values from multiple sources. Data fusion tasks belong to two main categories: single-truth scenarios, where each attribute has only one correct value, and multi-truth scenarios, where multiple values can be valid simultaneously. This paper investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in data fusion tasks for tabular data. Various prompting strategies, encompassing both single-truth and multi-truth scenarios, are investigated empirically. Domain-dependent, domain-independent, zero-shot and one-shot prompts are evaluated on three different benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that LLM-based approaches outperform traditional unsupervised truth discovery methods, such as DART and LTM, across all datasets. The codebase of this study has been made publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers introduce OperatorSHAP, a grid-agnostic method for fast and accurate Shapley value estimation in neural operators, enabling consistent attributions across irregular grids and resolutions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OperatorSHAP: Fast and Accurate Shapley Value Estimation for Neural Operators
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OperatorSHAP, a novel grid-agnostic method for efficiently estimating Shapley values in neural operators, which are crucial for interpreting model predictions in physical applications like structural load assessment and weather forecasting. This approach overcomes limitations of existing methods that require homogeneous inputs, enabling consistent and accurate attributions across irregular grids and varying resolutions without retraining.

OperatorSHAP introduces a training procedure similar to FastSHAP but extends its applicability to neural operators handling irregular data. The method is grounded in a theoretical framework connecting attributions in function space to Aumann-Shapley values, ensuring that its explanations align with state-of-the-art discrete Shapley values and transfer effectively across different grid sizes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding model predictions is essential for physical applications, where outputs often inform safety-critical decisions, such as structural load assessment, weather warnings, and clinical diagnosis. Shapley values satisfy many desirable properties as an attribution method, but their computational cost during inference hinders their practical use. Current amortized explainers, such as FastSHAP, are limited to homogeneous inputs, which is problematic for physical applications where data often comes from irregular grids and geometries. We introduce OperatorSHAP, a grid-agnostic attribution method and training procedure that allows us to train FastSHAP-like explainers for neural operators. We establish a theoretical framework for attributions in function space, connecting to Aumann-Shapley values. We further show that OperatorSHAP's explanations are consistent with state-of-the-art discrete Shapley values across resolutions and transfer across grid sizes without retraining.

items.title: Researchers propose ADC-GNN, a diffusion-guided graph neural network for few-shot fraud detection, showing improved performance on public benchmarks and a telecom dataset with 1% training data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Sparse Supervision: Diffusion-Guided Learning for Few-Shot Graph Fraud Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ADC-GNN, an Attention-guided Diffusion-Contrastive Graph Neural Network designed to improve few-shot fraud detection in graph-based transaction systems. This approach addresses challenges of sparse and imbalanced supervision and representation dilution by combining diffusion-guided feature augmentation, contrastive learning, and multi-hop spectral attention. ADC-GNN stabilizes node representations through noise-perturbed feature views and adaptively highlights fraud-relevant cues, enhancing detection accuracy with limited labeled data.

The model was evaluated on three public benchmarks and a proprietary telecom transaction dataset with about 60,000 records. Under a 1% training data setting, ADC-GNN consistently outperformed existing graph fraud detection baselines. Additional analyses explored its stability, training ratios, and resource consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency for real-world fraud detection scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based fraud detection is essential for safeguarding large-scale transaction systems, where undetected anomalies may lead to substantial financial losses and security risks. Real-world fraud graphs pose two coupled challenges: sparse and imbalanced supervision, where verified fraudulent labels are scarce and heavily skewed toward benign accounts, and representation dilution, where spatial message passing may oversmooth camouflaged anomalies while spectral filters may suppress fraud-relevant mid- and high-frequency irregularities. To address these challenges, we propose ADC-GNN, short for Attention-guided Diffusion-Contrastive Graph Neural Network, a unified framework that combines diffusion-guided feature augmentation, contrastive representation learning, and multi-hop spectral attention for few-shot graph fraud detection. The diffusion component is formulated as a feature-space denoising augmentation mechanism rather than a full topology-generative graph diffusion model: it constructs noise-perturbed node-feature views under a cosine schedule and uses contrastive learning to stabilize node representations across perturbations. The spectral attention module further adaptively emphasizes fraud-relevant hop-level and relation-level cues. We evaluate ADC-GNN primarily on three public benchmarks and additionally report a proprietary real-world telecom transaction dataset with approximately 60,000 records as a private case study. Under the 1% training setting, ADC-GNN achieves consistent improvements over original graph fraud baselines and four protocol-consistent recent graph anomaly/fraud baselines on the public benchmarks. Additional analyses on split stability, training ratios, oversampling alternatives, module-level ablations, diffusion schedules, and runtime and memory-consumption comparisons further characterize the effective operating regime of ADC-GNN.

items.title: Researchers propose CPAgents framework to generate interpretable composite cardiac phenotypes, improving disease association accuracy across nine clinical categories in population-scale imaging study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CPAgents: Agentic Composite Phenotype Generation for Cardiac Disease Association
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CPAgents, a novel framework designed to generate interpretable composite cardiac phenotypes from imaging data, enhancing the accuracy of disease association studies across nine clinical categories. This system integrates three specialized agents that identify statistical issues, propose medically and statistically sound phenotype expressions, and verify these candidates through rigorous evaluation, producing transparent evidence trails for each accepted phenotype. Tested on a large cardiac imaging cohort, CPAgents outperformed traditional methods in disease discrimination, achieving top rankings in the majority of classifier-disease-metric combinations examined.

The CPAgents framework addresses limitations of current phenome-wide association studies, which often rely on predefined single-variable phenotypes or expert-crafted features that may miss complex non-linear effects and interactions. By automatically constructing composite phenotypes such as polynomial, ratio, and interaction forms, the system enables scalable discovery of stronger and clinically interpretable phenotype-disease associations beyond expert-driven feature selection. This advancement holds promise for improving risk stratification and cardiovascular research at the population scale.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying robust associations between cardiac imaging phenotypes and clinical diseases is fundamental to population-scale cardiovascular research and reliable risk stratification. However, current phenome-wide association studies rely on pre-defined, single-variable phenotypes or expert-crafted features, which limits their ability to capture clinically meaningful non-linear effects and cross-phenotype interactions. To address this, we propose CPAgents, an iterative phenotype-Composition framework for cardiovascular Phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) that automatically constructs and validates interpretable composite phenotypes (e.g., polynomial, ratio, and interaction forms) from base imaging features. Specifically, our system coordinates three agents: (i) an Analyst that identifies statistical pathologies and nominates candidate transformations; (ii) a Proposer that generates constrained, medically and statistically motivated expressions under numerical safety rules; and (iii) a Verifier that evaluates candidates using multi-stage criteria and produces transparent evidence trails for accepted phenotypes. Evaluated on a population-scale cardiac imaging cohort, the discovered composite phenotypes markedly improve disease discrimination: across 72 classifier-disease-metric combinations, our variants achieve the top rank in 56 cases versus 18 for baselines, with gains observed across all nine clinical disease categories. Our framework yields compact, clinically interpretable phenotype formulas with transparent evidence trails, enabling scalable discovery of stronger phenotype-disease associations beyond expert-driven feature selection.

items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LLawCo, a new framework designed to enhance cooperation and task success among embodied multi-agent systems by learning and applying behavioral laws. This approach enables agents to reflect on past failures, identify misaligned behaviors, and incorporate high-level cooperation principles like "Talk when necessary" and "Wait for partner" into their decision-making processes through supervised fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs).

To validate LLawCo, the team developed PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale benchmark for multi-agent communication and cooperative planning. Experiments on this benchmark and existing tasks showed that LLawCo significantly improves cooperative efficiency and task success rates, achieving average success rate increases of 4.5% on PARTNR-Dialog and 6.8% on the TDW-MAT benchmark compared to leading open-source communicative agent frameworks across four different LLMs.

These results suggest that explicitly learning and integrating behavioral laws can better align agents' actions with both their partners and task objectives, potentially advancing the development of more effective multi-agent systems in decentralized and partially observable environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied agents operating in decentralized and partially observable environments have attracted growing attention in recent years. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based agents often exhibit behaviors that are misaligned with their partners or inconsistent with the environment state, leading to inefficient cooperation and poor task success. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework, Learning Laws of Cooperation (LLawCo), that enables embodied agents to autonomously align with both their partners and task objectives. Our framework allows agents to reflect on past failures to extract misaligned behavioral patterns, which are used to derive high-level behavioral laws, such as "Talk when necessary" and "Wait for partner." These laws are explicitly incorporated into the agents' chains of thought via supervised fine-tuning, aligning their reasoning with task requirements and the behavior of other agents. To evaluate our approach, we introduce PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale multi-agent communicative and cooperative planning benchmark built on the PARTNR environment. Experiments on existing tasks and our new benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in cooperative efficiency and task success rates. Across four backbone LLMs, our method achieves average success rate improvements of 4.5% on the PARTNR-Dialog benchmark and 6.8% on the TDW-MAT benchmark over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks. See the LLawCo project page for details: https://www.merl.com/research/highlights/LLawCo

items.title: Study analyzes 32 years of Sri Lankan remittances using machine learning, finds external macroeconomic factors drive inflows and projects 2026 remittances at USD 9 billion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Remittance Blueprint: Data-driven Intelligence for Sri Lanka
items.summary:
A study analyzing 32 years of Sri Lankan migration and remittance data from 1994 to 2025 uses machine learning and time-series modeling to identify key drivers of remittance inflows. The research finds that external macroeconomic factors, particularly exchange rate fluctuations and global oil prices, have a stronger influence on remittances than domestic economic indicators. The study's predictive models, especially Ridge Regression, outperform traditional methods and project remittances to reach approximately USD 9 billion by 2026 under stable conditions.

The analysis employs a comprehensive 384-month dataset and applies techniques such as exploratory data analysis, stationarity corrections, and impulse response analysis to confirm the asymmetric effects of currency depreciation and oil price shocks. These findings underscore the structural dependence of Sri Lankan remittances on global economic conditions and highlight the importance of robust exchange rate policies, skilled migration strategies, and formal financial channels to support the country's economic resilience.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study analyzes Sri Lankan migration and remittances over 32 years (1994-2025). Using a 384-month harmonized dataset, we apply exploratory data analysis, stationarity corrected time-series modeling (ADF, Johansen, VAR/VECM), and supervised learning. Results reveal remittance inflows are primarily driven by external macroeconomic variables, specifically exchange rate dynamics and global oil prices, rather than domestic indicators. Impulse response analysis confirms the asymmetric impact of currency depreciation and oil price shocks. Predictively, multivariate machine learning models outperform traditional univariate approaches; Ridge Regression achieves a 73.8% accuracy improvement over SARIMA (Annualized RMSE: USD 494.8 Mn). The optimized framework projects 2026 remittances at USD 9,001 million under stable conditions. These findings highlight the structural dependence of remittances on global economies, emphasizing the need for robust exchange rate policies, skilled migration, and formal financial channels to enhance long-term economic resilience.

items.title: Researchers propose a framework for value-constrained reward allocation in fully delegated AI cooperatives using traversal learning for decentralized gradient attribution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Value-Constrained Credit Assignment in Fully Delegated AI Cooperatives
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework for allocating rewards in fully delegated AI cooperatives, where human participants are represented by agents contributing data and model updates under diverse value constraints. The approach credits only those updates that meet each principal's value profile, using value-conditioned gradient filtering and online marginal contribution signals within a traversal learning (TL) system. TL enables decentralized backpropagation without the quality loss typical of aggregation-based distributed learning and provides more precise attribution than traditional federated learning methods by preserving explicit traversal and gradient paths.

This framework addresses challenges in data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment by integrating cumulative revenue settlement mechanisms. The use of traversal learning offers a novel substrate for decentralized credit assignment, potentially improving fairness and efficiency in AI cooperative reward distribution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a framework for reward allocation in fully delegated AI cooperatives where humans are represented by agents that contribute data and participate in model updates under heterogeneous value constraints. The key idea is to credit only those updates that remain admissible after screening them against each principal's value profile. We formulate value-conditioned gradient filtering, online marginal contribution signals, and cumulative revenue settlement within a traversal learning (TL) substrate. TL is especially attractive here because it performs decentralized backpropagation without the quality loss associated with aggregation-centric distributed learning and, we argue, offers a finer attribution substrate than FedAvg-style federated learning by preserving explicit traversal and gradient paths. The framework is positioned against data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment.
